speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN THIRD REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I have the honour once again, Mr. Speaker, on behalf of Your Honour's committee on procedure and organization to move concurrence in a report presented by this committee. I am grateful once more to the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) for offering to second my motion. There are three parts to the brief remarks that I should like to make on this occasion.
First of all, sir, I should like to say a few words about the structure of Your Honour's committee and the work that committee is doing. As hon. members will recall from the first report of the committee which Your Honour tabled on March 25, the main committee has been divided into three subcommittees. The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) is chairman of one of those subcommittees; the hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett) is chairman of another, and I have the honour of chairing the subcommittee on procedure. All three of these committees, as well as the main committee, have been working very hard on the matters assigned to them and it is my understanding that very shortly each of the other subcommittees will have reports to be presented to the house. On those occasions the other subcommittee chairmen will be moving concurrence in the reports. I should like to express my own personal pleasure at working on both the subcommittee and the main committee. We are tackling a big job with earnestness and seriousness, and I dare to hope that as the weeks go by we will be able to make considerable progress, as I believe we have done already.
The second thing I should like to say, Mr. Speaker, is to draw particular attention to the provisional standing order that we are asking the house to adopt by the motion to concur in the third report of the committee which was tabled two days ago. This new provisional standing order, which would carry the number 15(2-a), will make provision regarding the making of statements on motions. Many members may not even realize that
thus far we have no standing orders and no provision whatever for the making of statements on motions. This is a practice that has grown up, and tradition seems to rule the day. Therefore, by not having any standing orders governing this matter, Your Honour has to be guided by precedents, by incidents in the past, and by judging the situation as it arises from day to day.
It is the feeling of the subcommittee, shared by the entire committee-in fact our decision in this matter is unanimous-that we should have a standing order governing the making of statements on motions so that Your Honour will have something to go by. We feel that provision should be made for statements to be made on motions by ministers of the crown, but we feel that something should be said to impose certain limitations. Therefore in our proposed standing order we say such statements should deal only with announcements or statements of policy and that they should present only such facts as it is deemed necessary to make known to the house; and we add the proviso that the making of statements on motions should not be designed in such a way as to provoke debate at that stage.
In the standing order we add the provision that one spokesman for each opposition party should be permitted to comment briefly, subject to the same limitations. I think all members will agree that in practice we have expanded on this procedure, which was not provided for at all, and on too many occasions we have had a five man debate in which nobody else can take part, which leaves us all with the feeling that we have taken too much time and that we have not actually dealt with any item of the business before the house.
I could, but I am not going to, cite examples of faults on both sides of the house. I have gone out of my way to speak to some of the front benchers on both sides of the house, and I find there is general agreement that we could improve this item of our business to the advantage of the house as a whole. I hope the house will accept the motion for the concurrence in this report; that it will accept this proposed standing order; that with the cooperation of the members we can get away from having irregular debates on statements made on motions and that we can have instead, when they are necessary, statements of fact from the government side and brief comment from spokesmen on the opposition side of the house.

Procedure Committee
The third thing I would like to say is that I hope hon. members will look at this proposal in the context of what this committee has endeavoured to present to the house thus far. As time goes on we shall have other proposals to bring in, but thus far we have been dealing with what I think is a justifiable criticism, that the house has been taking too long with its preliminaries, that it has been taking too long to get down to the business of the day.
We agree that questions are an important part of the house business. So are statements on motions and motions for the production of papers, but to the extent that we have taken an hour and even two hours on these preliminaries we have created the impression of being too slow in getting down to the business of the house. We feel that by a combination of our proposals thus far, what we have done about questions and what we now propose to do about motions, we can reach the point where we will get down to the day's business sooner, we can offset the criticism about spending too long on preliminaries, we can improve the image of the house and we can, in fact, get down to our work that much quicker.
We propose that this provisional standing order should be in effect from the date on which this motion is concurred in until the end of the session, unless otherwise ordered by the house itself, and our committee hopes that the house will adopt this rule unanimously.

Mr. Speaker, briefly I want to say that 1 approve as far as I can personally the recommendation contained in this report and the trial for a limited period of what is proposed, but may I briefly recite the philosophy which we have with regard to these particular changes, because there has been considerable comment in the house and outside in the press and elsewhere.
I think it is safe to say that those who suggest that hon. members come to this house purely to pass government measures or pass government estimates are wrong. We are here to give lengthy and critical examination to all matters which are on the order paper for debate. Only in this way does the public get the opportunity to examine in detail the subject matters which the house debates from time to time. It is only through the cut and thrust and the give and take of debate that this happens. Anyone who thinks there is not going to be a continuous series of wars, battles and skirmishes in this house is very wide of the mark.
On the other hand, those who suggest that there should be a continuous donnybrook

without rules, rhyme or reason are also wrong. I think we have to stop occasionally to drag out the bodies and put fresh sawdust in the ring, take time to find out what the new issues will be and when and where we wish to join them. It is in this sense, trying to reconcile those two opposing views, that the committee and the subcommittee have approached this problem of dealing with our rules.
There must be continuous review of and changes in the rules. With regard to this suggested amendment, what we are doing is legalizing a custom which has existed for some time. Frequently we have found that putting a custom into written words is a dangerous practice. It is often better to allow those customs to be moulded and refined by what happens. But I think, unfortunately, over the last period of time we have found that statements and comments on motions have been taking up a considerable part of the time of this house, so we are recommending this for a period of trial in the hope that there may be some measure of improvement.
I think it is a question of practicing self restraint. As a backbencher this direction has often been given to me. I think it would be helpful to bring it to the notice of those who sit on the front benches opposite particularly, from where these motions originate. I propose to them that they bear in mind the motto hung up in railway stations during the war: "Is your journey really necessary?" They might ask themselves, before making statements: "Are these statements really necessary?" After they are made, it frequently happens that no reply may be necessary at all from the opposition side. Frequently one reply only might be sufficient; and those who have in the past directed to us the admonition that we should save the time of the house might give this some consideration.
Finally, we are departing to some extent from the English practice. There is no reason why we should slavishly follow English practice but in England, in the mother of parliaments, these statements on motions are followed not only by comments, but questions are allowed. In this way the issue is sharpened and clarified so that it becomes quite apparent what is involved in the statement. Because of the situation in this house, the number of parties and the type of statements which have been made, it is not possible to follow that practice, but I hope that after giving careful consideration to what happens when this rule comes into effect the word "comment" which appears in the second last line in the phrase "parties in opposition to the government may

comment briefly" might be extended to include the right of questioning. This is something that will have to be considered in due course. This procedure might then serve a very useful purpose in preparing these particular subject matters for consideration and future debate.

On occasion we believe there has been far too much preamble to the actual statement of fact or policy being presented, and on other occasions there has been too much debate from all parties in opposition.
We believe that in the majority of cases the acceptance of this motion will not require any action on the part of the Speaker, but we think it is necessary to have this provision in standing orders so that Your Honour's position will be strengthened in dealing with a situation that gets out of hand when statements are made on motions.

maintopic: CHANGE IN ADMINISTRATION OF DELIVERY QUOTAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Trade and Commerce I should like to try to make a statement subject to the new rule. I wish to inform the house of a change in the administration of the delivery quotas of grain in western Canada which has been announced today by the Canadian wheat board. The wheat board's announcement is as follows.
The Canadian wheat board wishes to announce a basic change in its administration of delivery quotas. Effective on Monday May 11 all delivery points in western Canada currently on an 8 bushel per specified acreage quota will be given a supplementary 5 bushel per seeded acre quota for wheat deliveries, other than Durum. As delivery points in western Canada are raised to an 8 bushel per specified acre level they will automatically be placed on a 5 bushel per seeded acre quota for wheat. The supplementary quota for wheat, other than Durum, will be raised above this level if and when the export and domestic movement of wheat warrants an increase.
With respect to Durum wheat, oats and barley, no further deliveries of these grains will be allowed beyond the 8 bushel per specified acre level unless market demand for these grains warrants quota increases. In this event it will be the board's intention to grant supplementary quotas for the grain required.
The basic reason for this change in policy is that the board must have the type of grain in the marketing pipe line that is required to meet market requirements. Extremely heavy commitments for wheat other than Durum have been entered into for delivery prior to the end of the crop year. To facilitate the movement of this wheat and to avoid congesting marketing facilities with grain that is not immediately required for the market, the board deems this change in quota policy to be essential.
With respect to oats, barley and Durum wheat, the board wishes to call attention to the fact that producers can deliver these

grains up to the 8 bushel per specified acre level. This level is comparable to the quota level normally existing in the past few years at the end of the crop year.

maintopic: CHANGE IN ADMINISTRATION OF DELIVERY QUOTAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the statement made today by the Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce regarding the new policy on quotas indicates the wisdom of certain statements made last year to the effect that there was a market for grains, and that if all the grain was sold there would be no question of having these quotas at all.
This is not exactly the free quota which we had two years ago, but it is a big step toward it. I think we all feel a little sad that the producers of oats, barley and Durum wheat are not in the position where they can deliver above the 8 bushel quota. It is no great satisfaction to them to be told that this quota is similar to what it used to be. Farmers now know that there is a market for their products in the world and they want to see that everything is done to make sure their products get to the markets.
I would hope that in the future no more statements would be made that might lead farmers to reduce production on the ground of the lack of markets, and that no more statements will be made saying that markets have had to be turned down, as happened this year, because there were not shipping facilities out of the country.
In summary, we are very glad to see the quotas moving up to a fairly nice figure, and we hope that something will happen to bring a little better news to the oats, barley and Durum wheat producers.

Unfortunately time did not permit me to place all the facts on record for the minister's guidance. I will say to him now, though, that my information is that when Mr. Trach was requested to cut his contract, that is his contract to supply milk and ice cream to stations Namao and Griesbach, he was told there were certain elements and certain people who stated that if Trach did not agree to the contract being reduced from six months to three months "the Department of Agriculture could make it very difficult for us". That was Mr. McKay; and Mr. McKay, it should be said, is not an employee of the Minister of Agriculture; he is an employee of the Minister of Defence Production who I see, is sitting beside the Minister of Agriculture now, perhaps the better to make the explanations which are required.
Mr. McKay, at this particular interview of which I spoke, the employee of the Minister of Defence Production, then referred to the federal Department of Agriculture at Ottawa and particularly to the minister, that is the Minister of Agriculture; and Mr. McKay stated that he had instructions that the minister, that is the Minister of Agriculture, wanted the contract cut.
It is admirable that there should be cooperation between one department and another, but if my information is correct this is the wrong kind of co-operation when we have the Minister of Agriculture instructing an employee of the Minister of Defence Production in this fashion. Mr. Trach, I am

informed, told Mr. McKay that in his opinion the Department of Agriculture could not break the contract nor could the Department of Defence Production, since it was in writing and properly executed. Mr. Chairman, I shall try to be more concise than the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. NielsenX
A country has never been prosperous without a flourishing agriculture, and especially in a country where agriculture is prominent in the economic life, as is precisely the case for Canada, a country where agriculture is extremely diversified, where farm yields are enormous and could even be bigger, if all agricultural fields were developed adequately all across the country.
Canada has a Minister of Agriculture whose responsibility includes a farm production infinitely diversified on a territory as broad as a continent. The great importance given to agriculture in western Canada, on account of its enormous production of wheat and grains,

has often led people to believe that the Canadian agriculture boiled down to that.
Except in a few cases, the Minister of Agriculture has always been a member from western Canada, well informed in matters related to wheat and inclined, of course, to think that all other matters are of secondary importance, although food consumption on the island of Montreal, for instance, is greater than in the three western provinces put together.
We recognized that this situation had to stop and that, although it was good for the prosperity of two or three provinces, it played against the whole country's economy and prosperity. The prosperity of western Canada cannot guarantee the prosperity of the whole country, and the rest of the country cannot remain at the mercy of conditions which result in an excellent crop one year and a poor one or none at all the next. The present Liberal government recognized and claimed that the agricultural situation in Canada, because of the size of our country and the diversity of its production, could not be directed efficiently by a single department.
We had stated that an important aspect of our policy would be to give eastern Canada its own minister, who would be entirely responsible for part of the farming development in the east and who would look after raising the standard of living of our farmers, by promoting full efficiency in agricultural and rural activities, which is an essential factor of prosperity, development and progress of our economy.
For the eastern farmer the dairy industry is just as important as the wheat crop for the western farmer. He cannot prosper without the development of his herds. It matters little whether he has the best cattle, the largest and best pasturage if he cannot market his products adequately, if he does not know how to transfer his dairy industry so as to make it more profitable.
The western provinces do not use up all of their wheat, they sell it to the whole world. The grain from western Canada helps to feed hundreds of millions of people, and we can but rejoice to see Canada, and specially the Liberal government, selling so much wheat and other grains to all parts of the world.
This however should not make us lose sight of the fact that in the other half of Canada, where we live, there are immense areas with tremendous possibilities for the dairy industry, and the raising of cattle. Wide markets exist in other continents for our products; and, yet, the yield of that form of agricultural activity is not what it could be; a part of the population in the areas where these activities could be carried on and expanded, does not earn enough to provide for

its essential needs. This is the new task that has been assigned to the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve), so that he will take care of this serious situation.
The problem is not that this part of the country cannot put agriculture and farms on a profitable basis. The simple fact is that agriculture in eastern Canada has never been given its rightful place, even if the opposition seems to find today solutions to all the problems which it could not settle when it was in power.
The possibilities of a country are not only measured by the amount of wheat or grain it can produce. We cannot take into account only one form of farm products and exclude all others. We must think of the whole and of all its component parts.
The fact is that eastern Canada has all it needs to put agriculture to the forefront. Vast areas are available for the kind of agriculture which would bring them greater prosperity. Some residents of eastern Canada have been living there for a long time; they offer guarantees of stability which perhaps have no equal anywhere in the country.
The people of eastern Canada do not have to become farmers. They are farmers by tradition and heredity, and a large number of them ask for nothing better than to remain farmers, providing they can make a living out of the soil and other related industries. Let us see the situation under its true light, however. If so many farms are abandoned, it is not because the soil is exhausted but because the families who had settled there could no longer make a living on those farms.
What is the use of having the best dairy herds in the world, the finest livestock in the country, if you cannot earn a decent living? You will have to live from hand to mouth, you will be compelled to stop fertilizing your fields and your pastures. Your property will start to run down; your family will be unable to live on the farm; one by one, your children will leave for the city, quite often without adequate training to earn a living. You will be left without the necessary help. With your children gone, you will not have the means to hire outside help and everything will go to pot.
All around you everybody is suspicious and pessimistic. Everybody says: what is the use of staying on the farm if nobody cares for us, if nobody does anything to help us.
I very often visit my riding which is partly rural. I see fine farms, fine herds, and a population which is sound, strong and skilled in all farming activities. But what concern, what pessimism among many of those farmers. They are wondering why they should remain on the farm and stick to farming.

Supply-Agriculture
Under the strong leadership of a minister whose purpose is to remedy so much misery, we wish to restore the confidence of our people. We must see, judge and act. Everything cannot be done overnight, especially in view of the slowness of this house.
In order to cope with the situation, we needed a minister who will deal especially with that poverty, a minister who will be completely aware of the rural situation, of its problems and possibilities, who will know the rural population, their requirements and what they can offer in terms of character, initiative, sustained work; a minister whose everyday concern would be to work so as to develop and revive that agriculture and promote its expansion, in order to obtain a proper efficiency, and who would move heaven and earth to ensure its maintenance.
Every week, commercial and economic missions come to Canada. Every week, similar missions are leaving Canada. The day when such missions will concern themselves with the lot of eastern farming, we can start thinking there is a will to do something with a view to the prosperity and welfare of a part of the people of eastern Canada.
Most recent surveys indicate that the number and the percentage of unemployed people are larger in the east than they are in the west. Would it not be because we have failed to see the situation under its true light, especially for the last five years?
There is only one way to make agriculture, which is quite different in eastern Canada, a prosperous, living and lasting industry. On the one hand, it must be organized so that the farmer will make a living by finding permanent markets and exporting his products. On the other hand, we also need a government aware and convinced of its responsibilities, a minister whose constant concern and essential task will be to organize accordingly his activity and that of the agencies under his responsibility, namely rural development, especially ARDA, by making it immediately more flexible and effective. Once agriculture is put back again on a sound economic basis and assured, by its own nature, of its future development, it is the organization of economic markets which will enable it to go ahead.
To secure our foreign markets is to guarantee full employment at home. Our recent wheat sales to the Soviet union, Bulgaria, communist China, Czechoslovakia represent a fantastic transaction, if we think of eastern Canada, and we are very happy about it.
The agricultural policy has been very successful for the west of the country. We are able to do as well for eastern Canada, where farming also has a bright future, provided a

special and essential part of the operations is in the hands of a minister who knows those possibilities and endeavours to take advantage of them as much as possible.
Agriculture has a double purpose, that is to feed a nation and, the economic purpose, to create markets in the world to balance its credit and its prosperity.
In that case, we should grant subsidies and credit to the farmers who would convert their dairy production to something else, like beef cattle for instance. We should impose high standards for milk quality, the farm as well beef cattle, and control milk sales through a national marketing board.
There is another thing we want to correct. Farmers in general, and more particularly in the east of this country would certainly benefit therefrom, because they are not informed of prospective markets for their products. There are, for instance, many farmers who know, as I said earlier, that the European market has unbelieveable prospects for our farming industry? We need a quick and dynamic information service. We need a research council on marketing, on the transformation and production of vegetables and animal products.
I think some beneficial solutions could be found for our farmers by establishing a "control council" for production and stabilization of feed grain prices by eliminating speculation.
If we want to help our farming industry, we should give it our special attention. The farmer is often affected by excessive production, by instability of prices, and his products are too often the prey of speculators who benefit more from government grants than the farmer himself.
We must plan, guide and control the demand and production by means of statistics, so that the production does not exceed twice the demand, thus lowering prices, which forces the farmer to sell his products at less than cost.
The issuance of breeding licenses would rationalize production and probably eliminate an unjustified competition against the farmer, which often leads him into a financial mess.
Breeding should be the responsibility of the farmers and not of the white collar workers, so that systematic speculation might be avoided. It would also be appropriate to define exactly the farmer's duties and to outline his aims, as is the case among the professional classes and tradesmen.
Farming was formerly the world's finest profession; unfortunately, it has become an industry. Let us revalorize the farmer's role; let us give him a real professional code;

I believe that such a course of action would dignify the farming profession; as all other professions and trades, it will support a man and his family properly, without recourse to all kinds of grants, which are often but mere poultices, devoid of healing power.
We have started dealing with these matters. The farmers would not expect less from us. Economy in eastern Canada is the foundation of their concerted efforts. We would not really succeed in rehabilitating economy in eastern Canada without first grappling with this problem. The farmer must be able to make a living for himself and his family on his farm alone, without going to the city, for whole seasons, if not for the whole year round, to earn part of his income; there are many people having to earn money, who cannot work and earn their living in cities, whereas the farmer, on the other hand, should be placed in a situation allowing him to ensure amply his subsistence through the sole income to be drawn from his farm. Such a policy of economic balance is essential if Canada is to have the economic and social security it needs in order to be a happy country in which each social class enjoys the well-being it is entitled to.
There is another very important point I wish to emphasize in order to show you that the French Canadian farmer does not feel at home in Ottawa but rather like a stranger.
French Canadian farmers, who make up 30 per cent of the farmers of Canada, cannot make themselves understood in the Department of Agriculture, because the very great majority of the civil servants in Ottawa, if not all, do not speak French but only English. There has been only a little improvement up to now. We cannot insist that English Canadian farmers speak French or that French Canadian farmers speak English, but we could insist that both be understood by civil servants, who are their employees.
If we really want to have unity, recognition of equal rights for both nations, parliament must develop bilingualism more intensely so as to include our farmers.
Our farmers believe in our Liberal government because we do not want speeches only but action that will satisfy all the aspirations of our Canadian farmers.

Mr. Chairman, I see there are just a few minutes at my disposal before we call it five o'clock. Perhaps that is indeed fortunate, because in my 30 pages of notes here I have a paragraph of commendation and 29 pages of condemnation. Perhaps I can get the commendation on the record before five o'clock. When the Minister of Agriculture gave his opening address on
Supply-Agriculture
these estimates it was expected from all parts of the house that he would deal with some policy in regard to agriculture as put forth by this government. The picture he painted in his remarks was, of course, of a somewhat rosy nature. He did state that the gross national income from farming rose in the last 12 months, for the year 1963. He did state and illustrate the importance of the research being carried on by the Department of Agriculture.
He commended the minister's department and we on this side of the house certainly want to endorse his commendation. Research in the field of agriculture in Canada is known throughout the world. These men are leaders in the field and certainly deserve commendation at every hand.
The minister dealt with an attempt by him and his department to bring the matter of research closer, in implementation and understanding, to the farmer himself, and I think this is a fine step to take. Too often have we had a tremendous amount of work done by the research department which would have been of extreme benefit to the farmers had it been initiated, but perhaps through some lack of communication, either on the part of the department or the farmers themselves, it was impossible to communicate this vital knowledge to the farmers. Therefore any effort made by the minister and his department to assimilate this information and distribute it among the farmers will be appreciated by all in agriculture clear across this dominion.
The minister also spoke of his activities in the development of livestock at the fairs. I think this is a step which is long overdue. I think the minister and the government appreciate the fact that the return of the fall fair to its former dignity, where we had greater emphasis on agriculture and less emphasis on the carnival aspect, would be of tremendous interest and benefit to all citizens of Canada. It should be a showcase for agriculture. We will have to wait, of course, and see what the new regulations the minister has introduced for the fairs bring forth. I imagine there is no reason to doubt that the minister and his associates will work very closely with the leaders in the livestock industry to set up these particular classifications.
I noted that the minister dealt first with the Hereford breed. I think he did this because the Hereford is a universal breed from coast to coast in Canada. The farmers in Ontario will be particularly pleased that he spoke about the fair in London and stated that perhaps this would be a good place to introduce such a policy, as far as dairy cattle are concerned. I should like to thank the minister for his praise of the cattle breeders in the

Supply-Agriculture
London area. We in southwestern Ontario think we have cattle breeders second to none.
Having said that, Mr. Chairman, I should now like to deal for a few moments with what is happening in the agriculture field today. Is the picture the minister painted as rosy as he says? Does this government know exactly what is going on in agriculture today? Are the farmers as happy and as satisfied from coast to coast as he would lead us to believe? I think the only way we can approach this problem is to analyse the situation. I never like putting a lot of figures on the record but I should like to illustrate what is being done.
The minister stated that the net income has increased in the last 12 months, and this is absolutely true. We all realize that the tremendous sales of wheat as well as other grains to communist countries have in the main been responsible for this. But when we analyse the figures which have been put on the record we find that the net income to the farmers clear across this nation, even with the tremendous sales of grain, has only gone up from 1962 to 1963 to the extent of $37 million. This leads us to wonder if all is well across the farm front of this nation. After delving into the matter a little further what do we find? Let us compare the incomes in 1962 with the incomes in 1963. During the year 1961-62 there was an increase in farm income in every province across the dominion. But what happened in 1963? In the province of Alberta there was an increase in income from 1962 to 1963 of $15 million. In the province of Saskatchewan, that great wheat bowl, what do we find? The increase in income was $97 million.
Now let us look at the rest of the picture in this rosy country of ours, this utopia for agriculture. What happened between 1962 and 1963 in Prince Edward Island? The income went up between 1961 and 1962, but last year it went down $130,000. What happened in Nova Scotia? Last year the income for the farmers was down $1.5 million. In New Brunswick it was down $900,000. And what about Quebec? This is the government which was going to bring utopia to the farmers of Quebec. Their needs were going to be looked after as never before. According to the minister, he said that the income from the dairies was the greatest since any time since confederation. Let us just see what the record is for the province of Quebec. The income to the farmers of that province went down $12 million.
What was the position in Ontario? We in Ontario were a little more fortunate: The income only went down $2,250,000. What happened in Manitoba? It went down $15 million. What happened in British Columbia,

that province on the west coast in which is grown all the wonderful fruits and vegetables and which has a great lumber industry? The income to the farmers in the province was down $4 million. Mr. Chairman, may I call it five o'clock.

The house resumed from Thursday, April 30, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mar-tineau:
That an order of the house do Issue for a copy of all maps, drawn up or deposited with the chief electoral officer or the representation commissioner, pertaining to the proposed redistribution of electoral boundaries in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, when I was giving my impressions, not quotations, a week ago, concerning this notice of motion-
-for copy of all maps drawn up or deposited with the chief electoral officer and the representation commissioner, pertaining to the proposed redistribution of electoral boundaries in Canada.
-the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickers-gill), who is not in the house now, said that the tabling of those documents would create confusion for the people, the hon. members and even for the chief electoral officer.
Mr. Speaker, that confusion was in fact organized by the orders or suggestions the chief electoral officer received from some ministers, either the Minister of Transport or another one, to the effect that he should prepare electoral maps which would be sent to provincial commissioners so that the provinces or the provincial commissions could take those maps submitted by the chief electoral officer, as a basis for their studies to reform or proceed to the redistribution of electoral boundaries in our provinces.

On that score, what I am interested in is certainly the redistribution of electoral boundaries in the province of Quebec, since I come from that province. Some others will have representations to make concerning the province of Ontario and other Canadian provinces, which will object to the fact that those electoral maps prepared by the chief electoral officer should be submitted to the attention of provincial commissions.
That is why I said a week ago that the Minister of Transport, as well as the chief electoral officer, should never have suggested that we go to the main office here in Ottawa to see the plans or drawings prepared by the chief electoral officer to give us an idea how the ridings should be organized or reorganized within the provinces.
When I called personally at the office of the chief electoral officer, I saw the plans, drawings and maps. They certainly do not suit me, nor do they suit the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau) or the hon. member for Chapleau (Mr. La-prise).
The chief electoral officer was telling us- and me, in particular-that for no consideration at all would be alter the plans he was then spreading out before me, and that the whole question would be submitted to the provincial commission which would decide whether or not changes were to be made.
Now, the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue requests that these documents be submitted to the house. If they are to serve as a basis for the Canadian provinces to proceed with the establishment of new electoral boundaries, as far as the province of Quebec is concerned, at least, I maintain that these maps must be submitted to parliament as well as to the attention of all Canadian hon. members assembled here in the federal house of parliament.
However, if those maps are not to be used for the establishment of new electoral boundaries in the provinces, the government should order the chief electoral officer to stop preparing maps and making plans for redistribution, since he himself admits that he knows nothing about Quebec.
Would the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) allow me a question?
With pleasure.

Could he tell us what would be the purpose of those maps, in his opinion, if they were not used for the establishment of new electoral boundaries. If they were not to serve that purpose, does he feel they should still be drawn up?
Electoral Boundaries Maps

In reply to my good friend from Pontiac-Temiscamingue I will say that existing maps should be destroyed.
If those documents are not to be submitted to the House of Commons, they should be done away with. It is not up to the chief electoral officer to decide the basis on which the commission for the province of Quebec should work, or, for that matter, the commission for the province of Ontario or that for Manitoba, the province of my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
The provinces themselves look after their electoral readjustment.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to draw your attention to the fact that when I called on the chief electoral officer, Mr. Castonguay, he showed me electoral maps. Taking into account-
Were you invited?

I went at his own invitation, for the information of my hon. friend from Lotbiniere. As a matter of fact, the Minister of Transport was also invited, as were members of each political party, to go and see, on the spot, the sketches prepared by the chief electoral officer.
Mr. Speaker, when I got there, I was told there was one map based on a 10 per cent tolerance, another based on a 20 per cent tolerance and, finally, a third one based on a 25 per cent tolerance.
While looking at the most important part of the country, that which, naturally, includes Rouyn-Noranda and the constituency of Villeneuve, I discovered that-
Our part of the country is also important.
-I discovered that we have in that area-a beautiful area-a region which is right smack in the middle-

speechtext: You mean the most important part of Quebec.

I believe my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre was there on one occasion, and he realized that it was the most beautiful area of the province of Quebec.
The cities of Rouyn and Noranda are twin cities. Now, according to the work done by the chief electoral officer-fortunately he is not the chief officer for Canada, but merely the chief electoral officer-Rouyn and Noranda are to be separated. Noranda is to be added to the Val d'Or and Amos area, and Rouyn, which is thoroughly "creditiste"-

Electoral Boundaries Maps with all due respect for my friend from Lot-biniere-is to be added to the Pontiac-Temiscamingue constituency.
While I was pointing out-
That is why the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue is afraid.

Mr. Speaker, I hear my hon. friend from Lotbiniere say that is the reason why the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue is afraid. He is not afraid, but from the geographical point of view, that redistribution would be meaningless and totally irrational.
At present, we have a constituency including the whole mining area in the northwest of Quebec. We have a riding that is fundamentally agricultural:	Pontiac-Temiscamingue. We have, to the north, the constituency of Chapleau which is also an agricultural, forest and mining constituency.
Now, when I met the chief electoral officer, I was introduced to the young man who had prepared the exercises, and both of them told me that those exercises would not be used to determine new standards or the new boundaries of the ridings in the provinces. However, they admitted to me that those exercises would be used as a basis by the provincial commission and that they will be used as criteria to determine in the future, in the province of Quebec, federal constituencies included, comprised and recognized in the province of Quebec.
When the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) said the other day that to produce those exercises or electoral maps to the house would create confusion, he was quite right. On the other hand, why did the minister extend to us a public invitation to go and meet the chief electoral officer to find out on the spot what progress had been made?
The chief electoral officer told me candidly, honestly and humbly that he knows neither the province of Quebec nor Ontario nor any other province in Canada. If we are going to set up ten commissions in Canada, if we are going to have one in the province of Quebec -I contend that it is the responsibility of this commission in the province of Quebec to decide what will the new ridings be in the future and to decide the boundaries of those ridings, and when this commission will hear the people who have objections in respect to such and such a map, or such and such a percentage of population-if we take for granted that the act provides that the average or quota, as we say usually, will be between 70,000 and 71,000 people per constituency-well, I contend that it will rest 

with us then to go before the provincial commission, and I am of the opinion that no member of parliament, no organization, no party has the right or the obligation to go to the chief electoral officer to see the basic work he has done.
We have been told that this work should not influence the provincial commissions, but we know that it will influence them very much and that these maps will be taken into account.
In my opinion, there is only one solution, which I mentioned a while ago, and it is this: If the chief electoral officer, with his maps, should not influence the provincial commissions, then he should burn them, and get rid of them, and we should hear no more about them. Above all, we should no longer be invited to see those maps, because it is an insult to all federal members of parliament. If on the other hand, those maps are to be used as a basis for future electoral readjustments, or the readjustment of future federal ridings, throughout Canada, then, the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau) was justified when he asked that these documents be produced in the house in order that each member may examine them.
I am convinced that every member will agree with me that the chief electoral officer does not have to take part in the redistribution of electoral districts. If it is refused to have these documents destroyed, then let them be produced in the house so that every member may know what is going on in his riding. I shall appreciate then the impression that the government strives so much to give us, namely that it shows a democratic spirit, that it allows freedom to every individual and also to every member of parliament, an undeniable freedom to every province of Canada and, under the circumstances, as far as we are concerned, that the commission has complete and unrestricted authority to decide what electoral districts must be represented in the house. At that time-

But, with regard to urban and rural ridings-

Mr. Speaker, I thank once again my hon. friend from Lotbiniere, but to answer the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, I will say that when the chief electoral officer explained to me the way he
Electoral Boundaries Maps intended to proceed and suggested that there would be four categories of counties in the province of Quebec, I was told on the same occasion that this whole question was resting upon mathematical and scientific factors, and that the population would amount to 66,000 for each county. At a given moment, when it came to the northern counties, those of Saguenay and Chapleau, the mathematical element disappeared completely and was replaced by purely geographical factors.
The situation had changed completely. That is why I say to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that even if the representation commissioner sits on all provincial commissions throughout Canada, I do not think it is wise to entrust him with the establishment of the new electoral boundaries.
I would be in favour of leaving that matter to the provincial commission in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, British Columbia, Quebec and in all the other provinces even if the commissions then had to rely on the advice of Mr. Castonguay and his staff of experts in mathematics and geography. However, I feel that far from submitting to the provincial commissions the maps he now has, Mr. Castonguay should throw them away. In other words, if he does present his maps, then I agree with the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue and I support his motion calling for the tabling of the documents in the house.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to support the motion of my colleague from Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau) and I would like also to say that in the main we support the ideas expressed by the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette).

Mr. Speaker, I have had an opportunity to examine the remarks made on Thursday April 30 by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) and I can only call his argument somewhat specious in that when he says, as recorded at page 2775 of Hansard for that day-
-what the motion is asking for is something which has no relationship whatsoever, except as an exercise in map drawing, to what will eventually emerge, if there is any disposition on the part of this parliament to deal with this problem and to deal with it in any reasonable time-
-he indicates that these are merely an exercise in map drawing. If that is so, then I would suggest that the representation commissioner is derelict in his duties because, by statute, he is directed to produce maps. These are not an exercise in map drawing. He is directed by statute to do this, and therefore

Electoral Boundaries Maps there must be a purpose. No direction of this kind by statute can be deemed to be a nullity or a frivolity, and therefore these maps do have a definite purpose.
Since we are asked under another bill to consider what extent of tolerance shall be included in the statute, surely it is pertinent to the deliberations of the members of this house to see what will be the results of the application of a number of tolerances? There is no one better qualified or equipped to take the electoral map of Canada and divide it up into the various ridings on the bases of certain tolerances. Therefore these should become the knowledge of members of the house who, on the basis of an examination of these various maps, will determine what shall be the better tolerance to include in our new representation act. Otherwise I would submit to hon. members that we are being asked to vote on something that will be entirely theoretical.
On whose word shall we rely-on the estimation of the Minister of Transport, or as a matter of fact on that of any member of the house-that a tolerance of 20 per cent will have such and such a result? Unless the minister has seen the maps that have been drawn on the basis of a 20 per cent tolerance, then frankly he is talking off the top of his head and his opinion does not warrant a great deal of attention.
What I find rather difficult to understand on the part of the government in resisting this motion is that we, or a number of us, have been invited personally to go and see the maps. I quite admit that the government is not trying to hide anything here. After all, members from all parties have seen some or all of the maps.
I have not seen any.

The hon. member for Bur-naby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) says he has not seen any. Neither have I, but it is not because there has not been the opportunity, or at least the invitation.
On the basis that we are trying an experiment or a departure in the manner of drawing up the electoral map of the country, surely to goodness there would be no harm done in publishing the maps on the bases of 10 per cent, 20 per cent, 25 per cent or 30 per cent tolerances, or whatever they may be. After all, the electorate is interested. I simply cannot accept the argument of the Minister of Transport, as recorded at page 2776 of Hansard that constituents could not care less what riding they happen to be in or who is their representative. At least this is the interpretation I place on his words, and I do not know where the minister gets
[Mr. Lambert.l
that attitude. It is quite untenable, and I would say frankly, almost insufferable.
Certainly the people in my part of the country are interested in the proposed redistribution. They are vitally interested in what may be the redistribution of these seats.
If we look at what will be the ultimate act -and here, Mr. Speaker, I must crave your indulgence so that I will not stray too much from the interpretation of this type of motion that I have placed upon it myself-under the representation act there will be little or no opportunity afforded to the public, unless it is widely amended, to see what the representation is going to be. Once the representation commissioners have gone to work they will compile a complete report, and once that report has been compiled it will be most difficult for anyone to persuade the commissioners that they have been in error and that they must make a change. Frankly, if the commissioners are not to use these maps -and we know that by virtue of the other act they are entitled to hire staff and technicians to assist them-then the direction to the representation commissioner is a nullity. Why would he prepare maps if the commissioners are not to use them in the end? It would just be an exercise in duplication. I would suggest on all counts, now that the representation commissioner has prepared these maps on the basis of these respective tolerances, that hon. members of this house who, after all, are not second class citizens, are entitled to see how the electoral map would be affected by these various tolerances, if only to assist them in their conclusions as to what should be included in the Representation Act. It would certainly be of great interest to the citizens of this country to see how the new act would affect the electoral map of Canada, and surely they have the right to know as soon as possible what the possibilities are.
I do not want to anticipate argument on the act itself but I can indicate, now, that the opportunities for revision provided by that act are extremely limited; in fact, they are almost nil. It is not good enough that this information should be limited, as it is now, to members of the house who can walk down the street and have a good look. If these maps were tabled it would be common knowledge how the electoral map would be affected and I think it is essential that this be done. Regardless of the basis used by the representation commissioner used in drawing up these maps-and I do not know what staff he has- I would certainly be much more careful in my re-examination of the drawing up of the electoral map if I came to the conclusion that his staff worked on some purely mechanical

formula and disregarded the other factors which we on all sides know must apply in the determination of new electoral boundaries.
On this basis I would urge the government to withdraw its opposition to this motion. After all, the Minister of Transport has indicated that this is not a motion of confidence. We believe we can convince hon. members opposite of the strength of our case. They know there is no whip lashing them on, and if a vote were to come they could support this motion.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
As I see it, this motion would never have been placed on the order paper and a request made for the production of the maps if the situation with regard to the work of the representation commissioner had been handled somewhat differently.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), who told us on another occasion that he had been working on this job for a whole year, perhaps misled the representation commissioner into performing certain exercises which may now turn out to have been completely unnecessary. As was said by the hon. member who preceded me, the Minister of Transport cannot expect the house to believe what he said on April 30, namely that these were just exercises which the commissioner was going through. I think the whole approach to this matter has been entirely wrong. The government has disclosed to us that maps have been drawn-I prefer to call them maps rather than exercises or tracings. Incidentally, I have not seen the version for the province of Manitoba so I do not know how the constituency I happen to represent will be affected. But I think the approach has been wrong. I think the commissioner should have started from the present constituency boundaries and, in preparation for dealing with the various commissions, considered in what respect those boundaries need to be changed instead of beginning the other way round with a mathematical exercise dealing with population and spreading out new boundaries all over the provinces. The rumours we have heard are that 75 or 80 per cent of the constituency boundaries are likely to be changed. I think it should be the other way round, and that constituency boundaries should remain as they are, unless there is some serious misrepresentation of the people taking place.
Then, I cannot help but wonder why the original exercise in drawing up these maps was based on a 10 per cent tolerance. Where did that figure come from? The bill before the house has a 20 per cent tolerance written into it; I know that the matter has not yet been settled by the house. But who gave authority to start from the basis of a 10 per
Electoral Boundaries Maps cent tolerance or a 5 per cent tolerance? If the representation commissioner thought fit to do these exercises, why did he not begin with a 20 per cent tolerance? Why did he not try his hand with the suggestion which came from Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition of 33i per cent tolerance? Why did he not use, as was suggested by the hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett), a 25 per cent tolerance? Instead, the figure of 10 per cent was selected as a starting point. This figure was mentioned in the house during an interruption when the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) was speaking, and, advocating as he was strict representation by population, he said: Ten per cent tolerance is what we favour.
Why did the commissioner select this 10 per cent tolerance as the figure on which he would work first? This is the type of thing which creates suspicion in the minds of members of this house and this is why the present motion is now before us. Who has been tinkering with this matter of redistribution? Why should we not have available for everybody to see these exercises in the use of the tolerance, so that we can make a sensible decision as to what should be written into the act and as to the instructions which this house should give for the guidance of the commissioners? I think it is of the greatest importance that the commissioners should find out from parliament what they are to do in this matter of redistribution. Unless the house expresses itself in directions and through the comments which are made here and which, I hope, the various commissions will look at; unless attention is paid to the act and these comments, the commissions might very easily be led astray and end up with redistribution maps which are contrary to the general will of parliament.
Why should we be kept in the dark with regard to this particular matter? How much better it would have been if the representation commissioner, taking the bill as it stands at the moment before the house with a 20 per cent tolerance, had drawn a certain number of adjustments based on that tolerance for the guidance of parliament. I think that would have satisfied the members of this house. Then we would be able to examine the bill before us to determine what is the fair and proper thing to do. Then we would be able to talk, not theoretically but on a practical basis with regard to the effect of redistribution. Then we would be able to see some of these great areas that are going to be affected in the northern parts of all the provinces, and the populations that are in those areas, and make a decision as to whether the tolerance should be larger or smaller, or whether we should take into consideration

Electoral Boundaries Maps the point which I raised in the earlier debate on the bill with regard to some allowance for area representation.
Without the actual maps it is difficult for the house to determine what to do. I have not the faintest notion as to how the maps will affect the province of Manitoba; I have not seen the maps. I do not know whether it will be a fair and reasonable redistribution of the population factor there. I do know this, that people in their provincial elections are accustomed to variations between the large areas in the rural sections and the more closely congested, city areas. I have heard little complaint over the years with regard to that. There was considerable complaint a few years ago in Manitoba over the lack of representation for people living in the city of Winnipeg, but an adjustment has been made along that line and I have not heard much about it since. The consideration of fair play is in the minds of most Canadians in this country, and people who live in the congested areas within a city understand that they are not too seriously affected if the total population of their constituency is larger than that in these great, extensive northern areas.
But let us have the maps in front of us so we can see what is the effect, because if the maps are going to be based on a 10 per cent tolerance I think almost every constituency in Canada is going to be altered. I would much prefer to work the other way around and show cause why any constituency should have its boundaries altered.
Mr. Reynold Rapp (Humboldi-Melforl-
Tisdale): Mr. Speaker, I should like to take the opportunity of speaking on this resolution introduced by the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau). I represent a constituency in a province that is supposed to lose four seats, and it is very important that not only hon. members who represent constituencies in Saskatchewan but also the people of Saskatchewan should know what is involved in this new redistribution. Unless we have the maps and unless we know what is involved in them, hon. members and the people of Saskatchewan will be kept in the dark. For instance, we know from the statistics that the four maritime provinces have a population of approximately 1,897,425 people and they are represented by 33 members; in other words, each member represents about 57,497 persons. The two prairie provinces which are supposed to lose members are Saskatchewan and Manitoba. These two provinces together are supposed to lose five members; but we have a population of 1,846,867, represented by 31 members, which is approximately 59,576 persons per member. As I have said, we are

supposed to lose five members in the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan, while at the same time the maritimes are only supposed to lose one. I am not saying that the maritimes should lose more than one member, because this is a different story altogether; they have the senatorial floor and other guarantees. For example, Newfoundland has the guarantee that it cannot go below a representation of seven members.
If we in Manitoba and Saskatchewan lose another five members, the representation by one member will amount to over 71,000 people. This, in an area such as Manitoba and Saskatchewan, will mean it will be almost impossible for one member to properly represent this number of people. We are an agricultural area and are considered to be agricultural provinces. I say, Mr. Speaker, that if an exception was made for the maritime provinces with regard to the senatorial floor, and if there was an exception made for Newfoundland guaranteeing them not less than seven members, why in this case could there not be an exception made in the case of these two prairie provinces which will lose five members out of a representation of 31?
I think we should have these maps so we may see what has been done, particularly when the maps have already been drawn. Unless we are able to study them, these two prairie provinces will not know exactly what is involved. I should like to see the adoption of the resolution of the hon. member which asks that the maps be presented to the house for scrutiny. If these maps had not been drawn by the representation commissioner, that would be a different story; perhaps we would not have asked for them. But since they have been drawn and since some hon. members have seen them-I have not seen them and as far as I am concerned perhaps I do not even want to see them-we should have the opportunity of studying them so we know what is involved. I simply cannot understand why there is opposition to having these maps laid on the table for every member to see. I know that at the last redistribution in 1952 there was a provision in respect of Saskatchewan that this province would not lose more than 15 per cent of its seated members. If I am not mistaken, at that time we lost two seats. If we are to lose over 25 per cent this time, in my opinion this is unjust and unfair. I believe these maps should be available to hon. members for study.
As I said before, I do not think that this is fair. These provinces should receive equal treatment. I think we should work to see that this is done, because it would be unfair if the people in Manitoba and Saskatchewan were to lose over 25 per cent of their representation through this redistribution.

Mr. Speaker, there seems to me to be some misunderstanding regarding what has been drawn on these maps. Some hon. members have contended that very large maps have been drawn. I do not mind admitting that I am one of the members who have seen some of the mathematical exercises which have been drawn, including census districts, which would in fact meet the tolerances set out in the bill before us. But they are not maps; they are not recommendations; they are not even suggestions that these are the boundaries which should be set up. They are simply, as I said, an exercise, some of them at different tolerance levels.
Unless we were to request that all of these exercises be produced there would be a complete misconception of where these constituency boundaries may eventually lie. If some kind of map is published with a 10 per cent tolerance and another map published with a 20 per cent tolerance-and even the tolerance has not yet been settled-this will lead to a great deal of misunderstanding. Therefore I do not see any value in having these mathematical exercises tabled in this house or in having them made public.
Furthermore, any member of this house can, as far as I am aware, go down to the representation commissioner's office and see where the lines are drawn on these mathematical exercises. There is no problem in seeing them. I know that some of them appear to be acceptable to me, whereas others do not appear to be acceptable to me; but if we are going to retain the idea that the electoral boundaries are going to be drawn by an independent commission, I think we must understand that none of these so-called maps are either recommendations or suggestions. I think there would be a lot of confusion in certain areas if they were produced. We would lose the whole concept of the placing of redistribution into the hands of an independent body and would instead give every locality in Canada the impression that perhaps this is the way a given map was going to be drawn, with the result that some people would object.
There will certainly be problems in moving boundaries. We went through this sort of thing in Alberta a few years ago when we tried to make the hospital districts, the municipal districts and the school districts have coterminus boundaries. Where I live there were a few sections of land situated in three different local districts. These sections were in Brooks hospital district, the Medicine Hat school division, and in a municipal district known as a special area which had its office in Hanna, to the north. We discovered
Business of the House
that the people who wanted to retain their traditional community of interest put more emphasis on hospitalization. Others were more interested in school affairs and wanted to retain their communication with Medicine Hat. Then others were more interested in municipal administration and wanted to retain their interest in Hanna.
The argument which was put up by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale (Mr. Rapp) to the effect that bringing these maps before the house would not make any difference to the number of seats which would be lost by any one province I do not think is valid, because the tolerance has yet to be settled under clause 13 of the bill. Furthermore, if we are to retain the number of seats we now have in the house and merely divide them by the total population, then Saskatchewan, Manitoba, or any other province will have assigned to them a certain number of seats. Where the boundaries are drawn after that certain number of seats for each province has been decided will not be either helped or hindered by the publication of these mathematical exercises. Therefore, as I say, there will be a great deal of confusion if one of these exercises was published but not the others.
I think we should also stick to the principle enunciated and endorsed by the house in the first instance, namely that we are going to take the matter of redistribution out of parliament and put it in the hands of an independent commission. If we get embroiled in the question whether boundaries are going to be moved a little one way or another, I think the discussion will deteriorate into an interest in local affairs and we will lose the over-all concept which I believe is a good one. May I call it six o'clock?
