speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. When the committee rose at five o'clock the hon. member for Kent (Ont.) was discussing item 1.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at five o'clock I was pointing out that, although the minister had indicated that the net income of farmers was greater in 1963 than in 1962 by some $37 million, most of which can be directly attributed to the extensive sales of grain, only two of Canada's provinces did in fact have an increase in net income over the past 12 months. I was dealing with the western provinces and we find that even in Manitoba the net income of farmers dropped $54 million in the last 12 months.
The figures I have placed on the record are only rounded and not detailed figures, but this is the government whose members went out on the hustings and said that their primary aim with regard to agriculture was to make the economic situation of the eastern farmers the same as that of the western farmers. Everyone believed that meant an increase in income. Today we take a dim view of the fact that western farmers, with the exception of two provinces, are in the same situation as the eastern farmers, with income on a downward trend.
I am one of the many thousands of farmers in Canada who feel that the opportunities for agriculture in the next 20 years will perhaps be greater than ever before in the history of this country. That is why I share the deep

concern and uneasiness of farmers from coast to coast over conditions in farming as they actually exist today.
What are some of these conditions, Mr. Chairman? Let us deal with some of them in some detail. What about cattle? Cattle are important from coast to coast. If we look at the record we find that the average price for cattle over the past 12 months has been considerably lower. When the minister was questioned about this in the house he pointed out, and rightly so-we must give him credit -that prices were comparable with those in the United States, and in fact somewhat greater. He also pointed out that the people of Canada today are eating more beef than ever before, and this is also true. But when the United States was considering placing quotas on imports of cattle he was asked what Canada was going to do, and he said they were taking a long look at the situation. They did take a long look at it and while they were taking a long look at conditions in the United States Canada imported from Australia and New Zealand 41,000 cattle. Surely to goodness we must have some definite policy with regard to some of these difficulties in respect of various commodities.
What about hogs? Hogs are also important in the livestock industry. The average price of hogs was lower in the last 12 months. If the hon. member for Essex South has something to say, will he please get on his feet?
I would be more constructive than you.

I will deal with the hon. member for Essex South in a few minutes. I have a few choice ones for him. Not only did the hog producers of Canada not fill the domestic market but there were $12 million worth of pork products imported into Canada last year.
What about dairy products? The minister stated that for the first time the consumption of butter almost equalled the production of butter. This is great news to the dairy industry because it takes off the pressure that has been building up over the years. But the government placed the emphasis on the production of cheese and we now find ourselves with 40 million pounds of cheese in storage, an increase of 10 million pounds over last year. I am not going to deal with dairy policy in any detail because some of my colleagues who are experts in the field propose to do so. I should like to pass on to tobacco.
What is the policy of the government with regard to the great $100 million tobacco industry which finds itself in dire trouble? We have a marketing scheme for tobacco and that marketing scheme is in difficulty. The tobacco industry is in difficulty. As a matter of

fact, the farmers are talking of voluntarily cutting to 55 per cent of production at a time when they should be increasing production. We find that conditions are forcing a decrease in production.
What about fruit and vegetables, one of the greatest industries in Canada? The men in the fruit and vegetable industry are looking with grave concern at the deliberations that are going on in GATT. I was interested to hear the Minister of Agriculture state that he spent a whole day with our negotiators on this very important subject. This is a most important subject because the Prime Minister himself said, in dealing with the negotiations at Geneva, that if we receive some concessions with regard to various products that Canada wishes to export we will have to give some concessions. The farmers of southwestern Ontario remember the last time this government wanted to play Santa Claus in that regard, because the concessions they gave directly affected the fruit and vegetable industry, which is most important to that area. As a matter of fact, their concessions in this regard set back the greenhouse growers and fruit and vegetable industry 20 years, and this was deliberately done by concessions in duty. It is most important that this industry be maintained, and it cannot be maintained if concessions do away with all the protection against imports from other countries.
What about soybeans? Surely the hon. member for Essex South knows what soybeans are, and surely he should be pressing the government to establish a policy with regard to the floor price on soybeans. What about the floor price on soybeans? In the last election members of the government stated it was absolutely necessary that the growers of soybeans and sugar beets should know exactly what the policy of the government was going to be by March, so they could plan their crops. The soybeans and sugar beets are going into the ground in my area, and yet the farmers do not even know what the policy of this government is in respect of them.
Now, Mr. Chairman, the agriculture policy of this country should be the most important policy ever conceived. Today we do not even know if there is a policy. We have never heard of a policy. As a matter of fact, when we speak about the development of the agriculture industry, we find the minister mentioning research. He spoke about the co-operation of the farmers. However, he did not tell this house that last year Canada imported about $635 million worth of food products, half of which could have been produced on the farms of this country. This importation occurred in spite of the 8.5 per cent protection our dollar affords us against these imports.
Supply-Agriculture
No wonder the farmers of this country are becoming worried. They begin to wonder what will happen if they lose this 8.5 per cent protection. What will happen to the imports of New Zealand and Australian lamb, beef, butter and so on? What will happen when we lose this protection? What will happen if we lose further tariff protection as the result of these negotiations that are under way? No wonder the farmers are uneasy. They have not had any word about policy from this government.
In a speech made in the west recently the Minister of Agriculture stated the government had not been able to put any agricultural matters on the order paper. In his statement yesterday he corrected that assertion and said he did not mean it. He meant that because of the slowness in getting business through the house he was unable to bring forward any legislation in connection with agricultural policy. I should like now, Mr. Chairman, to refer to an article that appeared in the Country Guide dealing with the convention of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture at Charlottetown. The article states that in addressing the convention the federal minister, Hon. Harry Hays, said it was time to take the next big step in the field of farm policy. He recognized this fact, but he indicated that the government planned over the next two years to introduce new provisions in the field of farm credit, crop insurance and a new plan to alleviate the capital cost of machinery. The minister refers to two years, Mr. Chairman, but the time is now. We must have a policy now. How can we plan for the future of Canadian agriculture if we do not know what the policy is going to be.
We are now going into the second year of this government's term of office, and yet not a single piece of legislation, with one exception, has been placed on the order paper. This one piece of legislation dealt with having two ministers of agriculture, one for eastern Canada and one for western Canada. This seems to have been a trial balloon, because the government has not even ascertained what the house thought about it. They have withdrawn it from the order paper. Since then we have not had one single piece of legislation introduced. The government promised the farmers of Quebec an eastern minister of agriculture who would be from Quebec. The government gave them one, but they brought him in by the back door. They had to divide the Department of Agriculture. They talk about the eastern farmer, who is the most trained technician, who has to farm under the most complicated conditions and with the greatest amount of investment. What did they do? They put his problem under the Minister of Forestry.

Supply-Agriculture
The farmers of this country have asked for direction and they got two ministers of agriculture. They asked for action in agriculture, and what did they get? They got a split-up in the Department of Agriculture. In referring to the split in agriculture, I should like to say we have one of the greatest departments of agriculture in the world. However, as a result of the actions of this government the senior officials of the Department of Agriculture did not even know what minister they were under for 30 days, and I call this the ultimate in confusion. Knowing all the complicated problems of the eastern farmer, they put those problems under the Minister of Forestry. The farmers asked for legislation, but as yet they have not seen a single piece of legislation brought forward.
After almost 14 months in office you would think that this government, which promised the farmers of this country so much, would be able to bring forward one piece of legislation of a constructive nature. We have been very proud of the fact that this government has carried out the policies laid down by the former government. This has been their policy in agriculture. There has been some moderation, but every time our policy was moderated it was done for one specific purpose only, and that was to reduce the expenditure of the Department of Agriculture regardless of what it did to disrupt the Canadian farmers' ability to earn a livelihood. I never thought I would be in a position to criticize the farm policy of my own party, but I do it to this extent; the farm policy laid down by the previous Conservative government was not the end, it was only the beginning. If the opposition does nothing else during this debate but arouse this government to some action on behalf of the farmers, the debate will have served its purpose and served it well. The activities of this government in regard to agriculture have made Napoleon's retreat from Moscow look like a Sunday school picnic.

I should like to speak for a few minutes this evening on the matter of agricultural chemicals, pesticides and insecticides and what seems to be happening in various parts of the world. As a result of the perhaps indiscriminate use of certain of these pesticides and insecticides in the United States, Sweden and Great Britain millions of wildlife in all forms have been destroyed. There are instances where all the young fish, the fry, have not come along and the fish population has been declining.
An intensive survey was made from Maine to Maryland in the United States concerning

ducks, blacks and mallards, and the significantly lower mating rate for these birds feeding on lands that have been treated with certain of these insecticides and pesticides was noted. In Great Britain pesticides are reported to be responsible for the failure of the golden eagle to produce its young. In California pheasant eggs taken from pesticide treated land have produced considerably fewer chicks than eggs taken from land not treated. In the state of Maine the landlocked salmon from Sebago lake have contained d.d.t., and this has increased appreciably their mortality rates.
In New York state, the secretary of the interior of the United States, Stuart Udall, has stated that studies have "demonstrated conclusively" that failure of lake trout in lake George to reproduce has been caused by the presence of d.d.t. In New Hampshire again d.d.t. is linked to the high mortality of lake trout fry.
In Illinois the pesticide known as aldrin was used to treat 80,000 acres in an attempt to wipe out Japanese beetles. It wiped them out, but it also wiped out meadowlarks, robins, brown thrushes, starlings, grackles, and ringed necked pheasants, and substantially reduced the number of moles, shrews, cats and muskrats.
In Alabama the pesticide known as dieldrin was used to dust an area, with the result that 15 coveys of quail disappeared and 187 animals of 51 species were found dead in the area. Again, in another area in Illinois, dieldrin was used to wipe out Japanese beetles, and the same thing happened. Many species of wild life have virtually disappeared, and in some cases they have completely disappeared.
In Michigan and certain areas of Wisconsin d.d.t. was used against the Dutch elm tree disease, with the same result. The robin population in one Wisconsin town was reduced by 86 per cent.
This problem is considered so widespread and urgent in Sweden that scientists there have asked for substantial funds to devise a simple method of diagnosis and removal. We are perhaps rather fortunate that this has not happened in Canada to such a large extent, but I would like some assurance from the minister that funds will be made available for research on the question of these pesticides and insecticides.

Mr. Chairman, I am more than pleased to follow the hon. member for Hastings-South because it gives me an opportunity to remind him that some 30 years ago I was in his riding, where I learned something about farming, and also something about English. I spent three years in his riding, and following him tonight brings back

memories of names such as Dempsey, Johnny Babcock, Pecks and many others which I am sure he knows. Having said that I may now turn to my mother language and make a few remarks with regard to agriculture.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to miss this occasion of dealing with the farming industry and to tell the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) what our farmers at home think of him, of his program and of this government.
Mr. Chairman, it would be no news to you if I said that our eastern farmers, and more particularly those of the riding of St. Hya-cinthe-Bagot, are most disappointed and confused, because the federal government seems to have completely forgotten them.
What a difference there is between the speeches of those hon. gentlemen when they were sitting in the opposition and their present actions. When they were in the opposition, and more particularly during the elections of 1962 and 1963, hon. members who are now sitting on the treasury benches stated that they had an answer for every problem and promised that, if their government came into power, it would be paradise on earth, and our farming industry would know an unparalleled prosperity.
Speaking of farming, Mr. Chairman, I want to put officially on record some statements which were made during the 1962 session.
For instance, on October 4, 1962, the hon. member for Argenteuil-Deux-Montagnes (Mr. Drouin), who was for a time a candidate for the position of minister of agriculture for the east, but who was left in the lurch and remained an ordinary member in spite of his ambitions, was always making sweeping statements. For instance, according to page 195 of Hansard of that date, he said:
I shall point out the unconcern of the present government as regards any farming policy, and then I shall mention the solutions, or at least some of the solutions advocated by the Liberal party to meet those problems.
And a little further on, he stated:
Our farmers are at the mercy of a trust shamefully constituted to exploit them to the fullest.
He was more particularly thinking of the dairy producers, and added:
As a matter of fact, the farmers from the economic area of Montreal cannot reach the consumers' market of the metropolis without going through some big dairies, which subject our dairy producers to a sort of unilateral contract called "quota".
And still further on, the hon. member repeated:
It is time our eastern farmers had someone to represent them and look after their interests in the cabinet.
Supply-Agriculture
Further on, he said:
We, Liberals, also propose to change the Crop Insurance Act so as to make it really available to the farmers.
It is not only in the west that crops are subject to weather conditions.
And further on again, he said:
We will also succeed in securing new markets for our dairy products by financing, after an agreement with the school boards and through the provincial governments, free distribution of milk in all the Canadian schools.
That is what a member of this government had to say when he was on the opposition side. And the member for Beauharnois-Sala-berry (Mr. Laniel), in turn, stated, as is recorded on page 2687 of Hansard of the House of Commons:
During the debate on that bill, it was suggested that grain elevators be built along the St. Lawrence river to enable western farmers to sell their feed grain directly to eastern farmers. I hope the Minister of Agriculture will not overlook these suggestions.
The hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Bechard) did his bit, saying:
Let us encourage and let us try, by every advertising means at our disposal, to promote consumption of our dairy products in their various forms.
How many children, for instance, even the most fortunate, do not drink enough milk, when attending school?
And urged the government to distribute milk in schools.
Apparently, Mr. Chairman, the influence which the members of the province of Quebec have in the Liberal government amounts to very little, for we have seen nothing in the present government policy to make us hope that, shortly, the present Minister of Agriculture will implement the suggestion made to him by his colleagues in the province of Quebec.
But you will recall, Mr. Chairman, that it was fashionable at the time to make promises to obtain votes. Then came the election campaign during which these same people invaded more particularly the province of Quebec, but also the province of Ontario, promising the moon.
Mr. Chairman, I have here several copies of various election programs of the Liberal party in which it was said, for instance, that a Liberal government would appoint a separate Minister of Agriculture for eastern Canada. It is well known that such promise was made in order to win votes, especially in the province of Quebec. At the time it was known there was no unity of thinking in the Liberal party, but the promise was made just the same, because it was felt that the votes of the eastern farmers would be obtained if they were promised one of their own would represent them. As soon as the

Supply-Agriculture
elections were over, a member residing in Outremont having very little knowledge, 1 believe, in agriculture, was chosen to be appointed Minister of Forestry; more particularly he will be responsible for administering the ARDA program, which, as is well known, Mr. Chairman, is a joint program which was initiated by the Tories and is specifically administered by the provincial government.
It is merely a wee bit of satisfaction which they sought to provide for a member from the province of Quebec in an attempt to keep the other ones quiet; it was with this mite of satisfaction that the Liberal cabinet hope to answer the purpose.
Mr. Chairman, I can assure you that the farmers of the province of Quebec are keenly disappointed, for they are surely the first ones to feel the adverse effects of a lying and hypocritical campaign which was waged for the sole purpose of garnering votes.
Besides, let me point out that I have had the honour of defeating someone who was being hailed as the coming minister of agriculture for eastern Canada, in Mr. Pearson's cabinet.
It was Mr. Jean-Baptiste Lemoyne who had campaigned for a number of years among members of the Catholic farmers' union, before coming out in the open in the constituency of St. Hyacinthe-Bagot, where farmers settled his case by defeating him with a 3,600 vote majority in the very first year of the appearance of the Social Credit phenomenon.
The other day, on hearing the great statement of the hon. Minister of Agriculture, a very genial man, I recalled the days of my childhood; and I think you must have had the same impression. Back home we used to have two auctioneers. Auctioneers are very genial and persuasive people. I remember, in particular, Pit Leclerc, who was an auctioneer at St. Guillaume, and also old Charles Arpin. Just like the hon. Minister of Agriculture, those two auctioneers could sell a piano to a man who had wanted to buy a boat.
It seems to me that in the way he deals with the farm problem the Minister of Agriculture would like to use the same system as auctioneers to lead the farmers to believe he is giving them something, when in fact he does absolutely nothing for the farming class.
A few days ago, Mr. Chairman, in introducing his estimates the Minister of Agriculture depicted a most enthusiastic and alluring picture of agriculture and especially of eastern Canada farming. According to him, everything was fine, dairy farmers were making more money than ever before.
But if you take a good look at the facts, you will realize, for instance, that in the

province of Quebec the farmers' income, for the year 1963 alone, was $12 million less than during the years the Conservative government was in office.
If we take a closer look at the prospects concerning the farmers, we see, according to a pamphlet entitled "Farm prospects in Canada-Spring 1964", a picture which is quite different from the one painted by the minister. I will not go as far as saying that he knowingly misrepresented the facts or misled the house, but I sincerely think that he is letting himself be carried away by his enthusiasm. Undoubtedly, because of his lack of knowledge of the situation, he gave information completely contrary to the facts.
According to the pamphlet I have in hand, you read, for instance, under the heading of "eggs and chicken":
A larger production at lower prices is expected this spring and this summer, in comparison with last spring and last summer.
Those are the actual facts. Yet, the minister said that eggs commanded a higher price than before. But the facts put on record by farming experts say absolutely the contrary.
Further on it is said:
In February the average price paid to producers in Toronto for class A large was 35.6 cents per dozen, as compared to 41 cents in February 1963.
In February 1963, a Conservative government was in office. I feel that the minister, before making his statements, should consider the facts and reflect on what he is going to say.
As far as chickens are concerned, again according to this pamphlet-
An increase in the number of barbecue chickens and a decrease in prices can be expected in spring or at the beginning of summer as compared to 1963.
Instead of improving, the situation is worsening. Here again, I feel it is my duty, since the farmers in my riding entrusted me with this responsibility, to tell the Minister of Agriculture to check the facts carefully before making statements which tend to mislead the people.
As far as heavy turkeys are concerned, it is said that:
In February, the average price paid to producers in London was 18.5 cents a pound, that is 1 cent less than last year.
Everything is fine. Prices are going down all the time, but we believe the Minister of Agriculture who says that everything is fine. Look at the facts: prices are going down, but the minister says that everything is all right.
As for the price of pork, here is what the pamphlet I have here says:
Pork prices have been $2 or $3 lower per 100 pounds as compared to last year-Prices will go

up during the summer but they will not be as
high as last year.
Here again, we have evidence that prices are going down. And the pamphlet goes on to say:
The national average price for class A pork was $25.48 at the beginning of March as compared to $26.77 in January and February.
Prices are going down, but everything is all right; the Minister of Agriculture tells us that everything is fine.
Now, here is what I read for sheep and lamb:
Following the small seasonal arrivals of lamb this spring, prices should increase until July, but will reach a level $2 less per 100 pounds as compared to those of last year.
Last year prices reflected the policy of a Conservative government.
About cattle:
Feeder steer exports have gone down to about 35 per cent of those of last year, but they should increase slightly next spring and summer.
In eastern Canada, veal calf sales have increased by 6 per cent and the very large seasonal arrivals should keep up until the end of May. Arrivals decreased a bit in the west and little change is expected. Prices will go down until June, but probably not more than $2 per cwt. lower than the price of $31.60 received on March 14.
There is good news for you. The farmers will merely lose $2 per hundredweight on their cattle.
Now, if you wish, Mr. Chairman, let us have a very quick look at the Conservative program at the time we were in office.
The minister would probably be interested to know that, in my constituency of St. Hyacinthe-Bagot alone, because they elected a Conservative government in 1957 and brought it back in office in 1958, the farmers received, through the 25 cent subsidy per 100 pounds of milk, the sum of $1,516,221. With respect to the 12 cent consumer subsidy paid to dairy factories in my constituency, the Conservative government paid an amount of $867,246. In addition, it paid $306,536 and some odd cents in subsidies to sugar beet growers. Those amounts total about $2,690,000.
Therefore, looking at those figures, one finds that farmers in my constituency lost more than $2.5 million by electing a Liberal government in 1963.
I do not exaggerate, Mr. Chairman, when I say that the farmers of my riding deeply regret that the Conservative party was defeated in 1963.
Under the Conservative government, what was the net income per farm in the province of Quebec compared with what it was in 1954?
For 1954, the income was $1,671 and. in 1961, it reached $1,946 under a Conservative government.
When the gentlemen opposite claim that we did nothing for farmers I ask them to consider the facts and also to imitate us. If 20220-193
Supply-Agriculture
they adopt the policy which we followed when we were in power the farmers' lot will improve.
Now, what was the value of the sales of farm properties in the province of Quebec for 1954, 1955 and 1961? It increased from $11,166 million to $18,606 million under a Conservative government.
I would have many other facts to point out to the house, Mr. Chairman, but as other members wish to speak this evening, I will restrict myself and touch on only a few matters which I wanted to discuss.
After having heard the Minister of Agriculture on several occasions say and repeat that farmers had obtained more money than previously for their milk since he became Minister of Agriculture, I take the liberty of putting on the record figures given by the dominion bureau of statistics.
As for the price of milk, in the province of Quebec, for the years 1953 to 1963: in August 1953, the price of milk varied from $2.34 to $2.56. When we came to power in 1957, the price of milk used to make milk powder, ranged from $2.42 to $2.62 and under the Conservative government in 1962 it went up from $2.75 to $3 per hundredweight.
As for the price of milk for cheese production, it went from $2.45 to $2.76 for 100 lbs. in 1956, to $2.85 to $3.05 in 1962.
These official figures tell eloquently what the Conservative party did while it had the responsibilities of government. I would ask the Minister of Agriculture to take those facts into account.
Now, just a few words, Mr. Chairman, to tell the house that the present policy followed by the Minister of Agriculture, as far as dairy products are concerned, has certainly been detrimental to the farm people who, as usual, are going to pay the costs.
It will be remembered that last year when he announced his new policy a few days prior to May 1, the minister said this new policy would result in a saving of $6 million per year. This year, when he announced his new policy, he said that it would result in a further saving of $3.5 million per year. This makes a total amount of close to $10 million, more exactly a saving of $9.5 million at the expense of farmers.
I would ask the minister to explain how he can save $9.5 million at the expense of the farming class, while claiming at the same time to protect their best interests.
I should like to deal in more detail with this policy which I consider disastrous for the farmers. It must be noted that the price of a pound of butter fat has dropped from 14J cents to 13.3 cents, which will surely result in a loss for farmers.

Supply-Agriculture
The 30 cents premium for milk used in the manufacture of Cheddar is also removed, being replaced by a payment of 3.6 cents a pound for Canadian cheddar of first quality. This can only cause serious disadvantages to the farming classes.
What will happen, for instance, to farmers who make every effort to produce a prime quality product but are unable to produce cheese of premium quality owing to dirty milk cans or unsatisfactory handling?
You realize that the farmer while offering a quality product will be penalized for an error of which he is innocent.
It is especially unfair for the dairy producers in my riding, because all of them really try to produce a better quality product.
I am of the opinion that the minister should revise his policy so as not to subject the farmers to an unjust treatment which might befall them on account of this new policy.
I ask the minister what would happen if a cheese maker ventured not to hand down to his producers the equivalent of 3.6 cents a pound the government pays.
Would the government take some disciplinary measures so that the farmers may not be deprived of their due or would the whole question be at the discretion of the manufacturer? I feel that this policy-like all the others which the government has put forward since it has been in power-was badly conceived and does not show any desire to act in the best interests of farmers. It should be revised and thought out again to render justice to our farmers.

Mr. Chairman, I must commend the previous speaker, the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Hicard), for the interest he has just shown for the farmers of eastern Canada.
I commend him for this interest, because we now need every person of goodwill in order to provide the farmers of eastern Canada, and more particularly those of the province of Quebec, with the income to which they are entitled.
At this stage of the debate on the estimates of the Department of Agriculture, I would like to make a few remarks concerning the economic situation of farmers in this country, and particularly concerning the deplorable situation which faces the farmers of eastern Canada.
As a matter of fact, the farm people in eastern Canada are clearly the most neglected members of the working class. For a very large number of eastern farmers, if not most of them, the situation is worse than

for the unemployed who get unemployment insurance benefits, because those farmers who work at least 15 hours a day, get an income which is sometimes lower than the benefits paid to people out of work.
In the light of that situation, in view of the almost exasperating slowness to introduce legislation to help those farmers, and in particular those in the riding of Bellechasse, who are among the most neglected, as I will prove later on, it is my duty to draw the attention of the house to the need for closer co-operation by all hon. members to alleviate such obvious human misery.
I should like first of all, Mr. Chairman, to give a brief outline of the agricultural situation in my riding on the basis of the 1961 census. It will be noted that the situation has worsened instead of improving since then.
There are in the riding of Bellechasse 2,002 farms, 1,373 of which are considered as commercial farms, that is farms with a gross agricultural income of at least $1,200, which means that 629 farms have a gross income of less than $1,200. In this latter group, however, 156 farms should at least provide a sufficient income to the farmer since, for the 1,373 commercial farms, the gross income amounts as follows: Three of these yield a gross income of more than $25,000; 16 only show an income of $15,000 to $25,000; there are 58 with an income between $10,000 and $15,000; 268 yield an income of $5,000 to $10,000; 186 have an income of $3,750 to $5,000; 289 show an income of $2,500 to $3,570. But most of them, that is 553, have a yearly income of $1,200 to $2,500.
Mr. Chairman, we must come to the conclusion that 42 per cent of the farmers in my riding have a yearly income of less than $2,500. These are farms considered as marginal since obviously such an income is far from being sufficient to cover the cost of administering the farm, paying school and municipal taxes, purchasing seeds, maintaining buildings and farm machinery, purchasing equipment, etc. and providing for the essential needs of the family, including the education of the children, a point which concerns me more particularly.
Mr. Chairman, I am proud that there should be, in the riding of Bellechasse as in the rest of the province, an elite of farmers, people who are fairly well off because many of them settled on the better farms and had the technical and agricultural know-how which enabled them to adapt themselves faster to the development of that industry.
When one speaks of marginal farms in Canada, one immediately thinks of farmland in the maritime provinces. I should like to point out that approximately 38 per cent of

the farmers in those provinces have a gross income of less than $2,500 while, as I said, 42 per cent of the farmers in my riding are in a similar situation as compared with 37 per cent for the whole of Quebec.
And there again, I do not even take into account the 629 farms whose gross operating income is less than $1,200 a year.
Mr. Chairman, looking at this situation it is easy to understand why the farmers in my riding are complaining. You must admit that they have every reason to. That is why I am as impatient as all the farmers in Bellechasse to see beneficial and logical farm legislation introduced in the house. I must stress also how urgent it is to recognize without delay the riding of Bellechasse as a designated area under ARDA and also as an economically weak area.
Other details must also be given to give a clear picture of the situation. I do not want to take too much time, but I would like to underline a point which I feel has some importance.
In our province, an average of six people derive their living from each farm, and the figures are the same for my constituency. The average is 4.6 in New Brunswick, four in Ontario and three only in Saskatchewan, that is just half the average for Quebec.
The 1961 census statistics reveal many other handicaps, especially as far as farm machinery is concerned.
All provinces considered as poor as far as agriculture is concerned suffer from a lack of mechanization. In those provinces-Quebec, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and British Columbia-the number of tractors, for instance, is lower than the number of farms, while in the other provinces, it is greater than the number of farms. A parallel similar to this one would be easy to establish for other farm machinery necessary these days, such as threshers, combines, hay binders and harvesters, etc.
Furthermore, a number of farmers have difficulty in meeting their payments on machinery bought on terms from regional agents. Unfortunately, several farmers pay on this essential machinery an interest reaching 15 per cent and more.
I believe this situation is due mainly to too strict an enforcement of the law when the farmers are trying to get loans from the Farm Credit Corporation. On account of the endless red tape and the constant uncertainty connected with getting reasonable loans, too many unfortunately, conclude arrangements with companies whose craving for profits knows no bounds.
It is, therefore, easy to understand that the dissatisfaction of a large number of farmers

from the Bellechasse riding, as well as from others, is based on real facts. I do not want, therefore, to go counter in any way to their legitimate claims.
One could produce many other facts that would obviously show the unfortunate position of the majority of eastern farmers; hence my interest in everything that concerns agriculture in Canada.
I deem it my duty to give an account of the agricultural problem as regards my province as well as my constituency. I suggest that such a way of dealing with the problem pertains to sound democracy, providing that I take care not to lean to narrow-minded regionalism. A democratic society must listen to those for whom the elected government has to legislate in the interests of the population as a whole without prejudice as well as without favouritism towards any social class whatsoever and without settled prejudice as regards one area or another.
That is the reason why I wished to tell my colleagues and the government about some of our farmers' problems in the light of official statistics, although they go back to 1961.
All of the Quebec farmers are not poor or backwards in farm techniques. My province has its elite farmers; they are progressive and well-off. Unfortunately, eastern farmers established on naturally rich land are an exception.
Furthermore, farm techniques have been developed so quickly over the past few years that many farmers could not keep up with progress, either because of lack of knowledge, capital, equipment, guidance or other causes.
I would like here to express my greatest admiration to the eastern farmers who have succeeded in making both ends meet, for not all of them are well located or organized as far as various advantages are concerned: their success is primarily due to very hard work, to their unflinching ambition and to their love for the soil they till. The love of those farmers for their work is a constant inspiration to all Canadians who have a sense of responsibilities and who do not shy away from hard work.
It is imperative that this government, throughout logical and sound farm legislation, help all eastern farmers as soon as possible, especially in creating markets and stable prices for agricultural products; that would be in the interest of the general economy of the country. It must be borne in mind that a higher standard of living for the eastern farmer means a higher standard of living for the whole of Canada.
Mr. Chairman, about ten years ago, a Liberal government set up a Senate committee to inquire into the whole problem of agriculture and into the means of making better use of farm land.

Supply-Agriculture
If my information is correct, that inquiry led to the passing of one of the most interesting piece of legislation by the previous government: the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act, known as ARDA.
This government intends to give as much scope as possible to ARDA. That is why this important service comes under the Department of Forestry, which has less to do and is less diversified than the Department of Agriculture.
The responsibilities regarding the needs for eastern feed grains will also be transferred to that department.
Eastern farmers are badly in need of ARDA. It is also very urgent for them that the western grain policy be revised and greatly improved.
As a matter of fact, it is absolutely essential that drastic steps be taken to eliminate completely and as soon as possible all speculation on that grain which eastern farmers cannot do without.
Mr. Chairman, I could not help but be deeply touched by the sympathy expressed by the former minister of agriculture, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton), during the brilliant statement he made when the estimates of the Department of Agriculture were brought before us. I also remember very well the statement he made last fall, on December 12, on the quite painful situation in which eastern farmers found themselves. He had every reason to maintain that it was a real shame for the Canadian population that the standard of living of one fourth of the farm people of eastern Canada should be so -low.
Mr. Chairman, you can be sure that I am convinced of the deep sincerity of the hon. member; there is no reason why I should suspect him on that point. However, I must say that his belated sincerity bewilders me since, to my knowledge, during the years he headed the very important department of agriculture, not a single major piece of legislation was adopted to help marginal farms which are so numerous in Quebec, for instance. Perhaps he meant well but what good are intentions without deeds?
On April 24 last the hon. member for Qu'Appelle said amongst other things:
Last December during my remarks on the estimates I asked the minister whether he had knowledge of the farm survey we conducted in 22 districts of eastern Canada in January. 1963.
I presume that the hon. member has drawn from this inquiry a great deal of material to build up his argument showing the sad situation of the eastern farmers for the speech he delivered last autumn. I have not read the report of this inquiry. However,
[Mr. Laverdiere.l
I looked into it and found, on page 46, a really surprising excerpt, I would say "shocking" to repeat the term used by my hon. colleague; this excerpt is as follows:

Comparing the same two provinces, Saskatchewan and Quebec, in the last year of record, 1961, the average net income of farmers in the province of Saskatchewan exceeded that of the Quebec farmers by 315 per cent. On the average of the past three years, which included a disastrous drought year in Saskatchewan, the net income of Saskatchewan farmers exceeded that of their compatriots in Quebec by almost 200 per cent.

And yet, faced with such a situation, the then minister of agriculture had the government pass direct assistance subsidies, I repeat, direct assistance subsidies, for prairie farmers.
Here are the details: In the main estimates for 1958-59, $41.3 million, in the main estimates for 1960-61, $40.5 million, in the main estimates for 1961-62, $40.5 million. However, I find no reference on the same page to the effect that such subsidies that were surely much needed, were paid to eastern farmers whose income was 315 per cent less than that of prairie farmers.
Moreover, in the same document, on page 64 of the main estimates for 1962, I find the following items under the Department of Agriculture out of $289.3 million in agricultural estimates:	"Assistance to grain
storage in western Canada": $49 million; "board of grain commissioners": $6.5 million; "Prairie Farm Emergency Fund": (deficit) $49.5 million; "Payments to western grain producers" (direct assistance): $40.5 million; "Redevelopment and rehabilitation projects": $26.6 million; that is a total of $172.1 million.
Therefore, out of a total of $289.3 million, $172.1 million were paid exclusively to western farmers, leaving only $117.2 million for the administration of a department of vital importance and for assistance provided to the whole country and moreover, here again, western Canada got its share like other areas of the country. It must be recognized that for eastern farmers, the milk was rather thin and not very nourishing.
It was buttermilk.

It seems to me that it would have been appropriate to show a little sympathy at that time; we might have today a policy of assistance to the eastern provinces which would be in full force and we would be now in a better position to carry on the work which would have been prepared.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I also thank all the hon. members because they have allowed me to continue. I feel that I must thank them.
Under the circumstances, I shall add only a few words to my remarks. I want especially to mention this: I do not want people to think by the remarks I just made that there is any opposition from those I represent, namely the eastern farmers in general, to the assistance given to and received by the western farmers, because otherwise, it would only widen the gap which has often existed between the east and the west. However, we have to recognize the facts as they are.
For the good of the country, of confederation and of agriculture also, there must be an understanding between eastern and western Canada. One region can help the other and each can complete the other, especially in the production of feed grain which is so urgently needed for our eastern cattle.
I insist, however, that justice be rendered to those poor eastern farmers who have a right to all the advantages that the Department of Agriculture can offer.
I urge all my colleagues in opposition to get the government to be generous in all the policies that might help the economic recovery of our marginal farms, much too numerous in eastern Canada. The owners of those farms have shown extraordinary courage until now, otherwise the situation would be even worse than it is today.
In closing, Mr. Chairman, I would like to point out that I heard a while ago about the appointment to an important post in the Department of Agriculture of a bilingual employee, Mr. Robert Thomas. French speaking farmers are not spoiled when it comes to getting services from employees who can understand their language in that department. I think it is the first time that a bilingual employee has been appointed to an important post within the last few years.
As a French Canadian, I hope that is only a beginning. Today's farmers, thanks to easier means of transportation and more active farm organizations, come here to discuss their problems with the officials of the departments
Supply-Agriculture
which have the duty to guide them and offer them the necessary leadership.
They come to Ottawa more often than before. On the other hand, I would like to see that farmers who come to Ottawa as a delegation in the next few years to meet with officials of the Department of Agriculture get more-as one farmer put it a few months ago [DOT]-than an English lesson.

Mr. Chairman, I welcome the opportunity of making a few comments on this first item of the estimates of the Department of Agriculture. I would like to direct my thoughts specifically to the problem of rail line abandonment. We from western Canada are particularly concerned about it, and when I say that I am also thinking of the ciitzens in eastern Canada. But because the problem has become more pronounced and apparent in western Canada I would like to concentrate on that area because I am more familiar with the problem there.
When the government came into office with the fanfare of 60 days of decision we looked forward to its carrying on some of our good agricultural policies, and to its putting something into effect so far as rail line abandonment was concerned. Instead of having 60 days of decision we had 60 days of indecision and indiscretion. In fact, it has stretched out now to 385 days of indecision. Responsibility, originally invested in the former minister of transport, now President of the Privy Council, was transferred to the present Minister of Transport and is now placed in the hands of the Minister of Agriculture. We are wondering what this will-o'-the-wisp policy really means.
I should like to put some background information on record and in order to do this I cannot do better, I feel, than quote part of a message directed to the Saskatchewan farmers' union on December 6 of last year by the former minister of agriculture, my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle. I should like to read some of this information into the record because I think it is pertinent and that it may help the present minister when he does decide to take some action regarding this problem:
We sometimes tend to forget that up until a few years ago westerners were deeply and constantly concerned over the steady spiralling of freight rate charges. Since the war the cumulative effect of freight rate increases in percentage form was staggering. This was one of the major problems faced by the new government elected in 1957.
To gain time to find a fundamental solution to our difficulties we put a stop to freight increases by paying a national subsidy to the railways. Meanwhile the royal commission under the direction of M. A. MacPherson of Regina set about the task of getting at the fundamental problems facing the railway industry. You will recall that Mr. HOUSE OF COMMONS
Supply-Agriculture
M. A. MacPherson for many years had been the acknowledged spokesman for western Canada, I think it is correct to say that he had the confidence of prairie governments regardless of political affiliation.
The chief western complaint was that freight rate increases were loaded on the captive market of the prairie provinces, the maritimes, and our northern areas. Competition kept the rates down in the heavily populated areas of Quebec and Ontario.
The royal commission saw this problem very clearly. On page 34 of volume 1 of their report these words can be found:
"The commission is convinced that consideration can only effectively be given to these and many other special problems in the light of the wider context dealt with in this volume of its report. First, there are basic and broad correctives to be applied through changes in public policy which are necessary to help the railways find their proper place in the increasingly competitive transportation environment.
The recommendations we will make in this volume will be designed to remove from rail shippers, particularly from those whose opportunity of using alternative forms of transport is limited or non-existent, the heavy burden of obligations left on the railways as a legacy from another day. By the same token these recommendations should allow the railways as business corporations to take their rightful place in the Canadian transportation scene."
To make the position of the railways viable and keep them operating, the report, in general, recommended the elimination of passenger service in those areas where the people were not using these services. Second, that the railways should be allowed to abandon certain light density lines or that the government pay a subsidy on those individual lines where it was in the national interest to maintain operation. There was no recommendation that the Crowsnest pass agreement be abolished, but a recommendation was made where the railways could prove loss that a variable subsidy should be paid to make up the difference. As I understand it, this recommendation means that in years when there is heavy grain movement on a certain line and no losses resulted the government would not have to pay any subsidy, but in years when there was light traffic the railways could claim for subsidy up to the amount of loss.
Now I should like to put on record at this point something which I believe is very interesting in view of the fact that the railways have made so many applications for branch line abandonment in western Canada. I will quote from the Globe and Mail of March 10, 1964. The heading reads: "Rail Revenue 4-Year High, C.P.R. Says".
The highest railway revenue since 1959 was reported yesterday by the Canadian Pacific Railway Co., in its 1963 annual report. Railway revenue was $477,197,937, compared with $453,169,224 the previous year and $477,806,000 in 1959.
This reflects the result, in a large measure, of the heavy volume of grain shipments from western Canada. The Winnipeg Tribune, dealing with the same news report in an editorial published on April 3, had this to say under the heading "Odd Increase":
The Canadian Pacific Railway seems to have had a pretty good year in 1963 judging from the annual report made public this week. Railway revenues-that is, the part of C.P.R. income

coming directly from railway operations-amounted to more than $477 million, an increase of more than $24 million over 1962.
Freight revenue accounted for $419 million of the total take. This represented an increase of $25.8 million over the preceding year or 7 per cent. Freight traffic volume increased by 12 per cent and, according to the report, grain shipments resulting from the Chinese, Russian and other wheat sales contributed heavily to the increase. But it was not only revenues that increased, profits increased as well. The net earnings actually rose by more than $6.2 million over 1962.
It's rather odd that C.P.R. freight profits increased at a time when grain shipments increased.
Now, this is the pertinent part:
The railways have long and vigorously contended that they were losing money on the Crowsnest pass rates charges for hauling grain. If this contention is valid, the railways should have shown a marked decline in revenues when they hauled record shipments of grain to seaboard.
Maybe the railway accountants should take another look. Or better still, maybe some outside accountants should sharpen their pencils in a definitive examination of the Crowsnest rates.
I think this is a very important and practical thought in relation to the applications which are now before the board of transport commissioners for permission to abandon large mileages of railway track.
I should like to continue by giving a little more background and then to deal specifically with the situation in Saskatchewan. First, I wish to discuss some of the factors which affect our thinking, and the courses of action now to be taken-I am quoting, now, from the address by my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle which I previously mentioned.
In the first place the previous government worked long and hard on a bill to put our views of the royal commission recommendations into legislative form. That bill was finally ready for introduction in the parliament that met first in September 1962. Being of such vital importance to the economy of Canada as a whole and to the grain areas of the prairies in particular, considerable effort was put into consultation with various groups that had heavy financial interest in our projected proposals. If took some months to arrange, but we finally were successful in bringing the railway companies and the grain handling companies of western Canada together in a meeting. There were extremely frank views expressed at this meeting, but the most important fact was the recognition of their mutual interests.
In layman's language everybody recognized the fundamental place of railways in our economy. The railways recognized the tremendous financial investments by the great grain co-operatives and private companies and thereby the need for a high level of co-ordination between the railways and grain companies in any plans for abandonment. Therefore this conference achieved the understanding that was necessary before any solutions could be expected. I believe I am reasonably fair in saying that there has been relative peace between these two groups even though by sheer economic interest there tends to be some continuing suspicion.
In addition to the pure economic interests there is the far greater problem of the public interest both social and economic. For this reason, in January 1963 the government called into con-

ference the three premiers of the prairie provinces. It outlined in general the principle of the federal government's legislation and the several methods in the act that protected the public interest. Then the discussion went on into the field that was not covered by the proposed bill and which could only be met by the utmost co-operation between the provincial governments and the federal government representing the public interest. This was the impact on communities, if railway abandonment took place. Certain types of compromises based on the circumstances in any particular locality were discussed. The pledge was given by the federal government that after the bill was introduced and its terms were known future joint discussion should take place that would lead to a co-operative solution of any difficulties that might arise. Once again I believe I am fair in saying there was general agreement on the method of working together to resolve difficulties.
I believe I am also correct in saying that from a consensus of opinion that before any abandonment took place there should be a study of western Canada, region by region, to see that any dislocations were kept to a minimum. For example in a purely hypothetical case, suppose that three or four lines in one area were operating at a loss the railways would put in requests that each of these lines might be abandoned. However, a study of the region might indicate that if one of these lines were abandoned the other two or three might become economic; therefore it follows that any decision to abandon should be made with the economic future in mind.
The above description of happenings in the fall of 1962 up to January, 1963 puts the events of the last 11 months into clearer perspective. The government changed in April, 1963. Naturally the new government would want time to decide on its course of action.
I think I have put enough on the record, Mr. Chairman, as far as the policy of the former government is concerned, to put this problem into perspective and to indicate that the groundwork was thoroughly laid by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition and his capable minister of agriculture, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle. As a result of this, we felt, as I said at the beginning of my remarks, that action would have been taken by the present government, but so far it has been a matter of great concern to western people in particular, and I think to all Canadians, that this very vital problem has not been attacked.
To put this matter into more particular perspective as far as Saskatchewan is concerned, I have in my hand a table which gives figures up to November 6, 1963. It deals with approximately 1,392 miles of railroad. That is a considerable amount of railway line, and it does not include a lot of the applications that we thought might have come in, because when I was a member last fall of the sessional committee on railways, shipping and air lines I asked the president of the C.N.R. how his figures compared with those of the C.P.R., and he intimated to the committee that the C.P.R. had been reluctant to date to bring in applications for rail line abandonment. I think this is rather unfair, for the simple reason that it does create a little difficulty in getting the
Supply-Agriculture
whole picture into perspective. I inquired of the witness why he thought this was the case, and he suggested that, possibly because the C.P.R. was a free enterprise company, they did not want to divulge personal information to their competitors. Nevertheless this table points up just how serious is this matter to the people of Saskatchewan.
The table deals with 31 subdivisions. I am just going to run over them briefly: Avonlea, Amiens, Aborfield, Bengough, Blewett, Bodo, Bolney, Beechy, Corning, Cudworth, Colony, Cutknife, Carlton, Chelan, Central Butte, Dodsland, Gravelbourg, Goodwater, Kisby, Mantario, Main Centre, Porter, Rhein, River-hurst, Stewart Valley, White Bear, Weyburn and Avonlea, Tonkin (Yorkton-Parkview), Tonkin (Yorkton-MacNutt), and St. Brieux. Going back, Mr. Chairman, and being a little more definitive, in the subdivision of Avonlea, which takes in Radville-Avonlea, there are five towns or villages, with six elevators affected. There are 217 permit holders in this particular subdivision. The six elevators have a capacity of 282,500 bushels, with an average turnover of 796,907 bushels; and 165 residents are affected. That just gives an example.
Coming to my constituency of Moose Mountain, we have the Blewett-Luxton subdivision, where there are three villages or hamlets, with three elevators, the total capacity of which is 77,000 bushels. There are 76 permit holders and approximately the same number of families. Going down to Corning on this list, which is the Peebles-Handsworth subdivision, there are three villages or towns, seven elevators are affected, with a total capacity of 289,000 bushels. The annual turnover is 975,304 bushels. The total population affected is 345 people.
Then dealing with the Goodwater-Radville subdivision, there are two villages, with five elevators affected and 164 permit holders. There are 193 residents involved. The total capacity of the elevators is 289,200 bushels. Going to Kisby, the Weyburn-Stoughton subdivision, there are four villages or towns, seven elevators and 198 permit holders. To put these figures of permit holders into perspective, Mr. Chairman, we have, under the quota system in western Canada, roughly
225,000	or 226,000 permit holders. Approximately half of these permit holders are in the province of Saskatchewan. Therefore when I say there are 198 permit holders in one area, you can see how adversely affected is agriculture in this particular subdivision when there are so many permit holders.
To crystallize this a little better I will give the total figures of the Saskatchewan applications to date under the C.P.R. and C.N.R. The total number of towns and villages affected

Supply-Agriculture
in the 1,392 miles of proposed rail line abandonment are 187. Just picture that, Mr. Chairman. There are a total of 426 elevators and 14,850 permit holders. These are people adjoining the proposed railway line abandonments. The total elevator capacity of these 426 elevators is 26,987,700 bushels, and the average turnover per year over the last 10 years was 49,556,124. This figure refers to the 426 elevators. The total population affected-this is the number of people who live adjoining these lines-is 22,588. So it becomes apparent that the social and economic life of a great many people will be seriously affected by whatever policy is adopted with respect to rail line abandonment. This is why it becomes so serious in the minds of the people of western Canada.
It is true that I, the hon. member for Mackenzie, the hon. member for Lisgar and the hon. member for Rosthern-and I could name a dozen other hon. members in the house-have been putting questions to the Minister of Transport over the past year as to when action was going to be taken. He always fielded these questions by saying, "We have adopted the policy of the previous government. We have declared a moratorium on rail line abandonment". The government figured this answered the question. But it did not answer the question, because this haze of uncertainty has been hanging over the heads of these people.
One might say: "Leave that well alone; why worry?" But let us take the elevator companies. They have invested a large amount of money in these 426 elevators. From time to time it is customary to repair them, and occasionally they have to be moved or even torn down. There is a pall of uncertainty hanging over their heads. They do not know whether to repair them or to move them. In some of these small towns and villages people have carried on a family business for years. Their forefathers opened a small business in the town which has been handed down from father to son for several generations. Their life savings are tied up in it. They may also have the post office as a sideline and other businesses tied in too. If it is a large town they may have several businesses in that town.
These people will be adversely affected if the rail line is wrapped up and their trading centre disappears, and they would like to know whether to take advantage of the small loans legislation introduced by the former government and modernize their plant, or whether they should try and open up a business some other place and re-establish themselves. Some of the oil companies which
[Mr. Southam.l
are developing in certain areas of Saskatchewan are using the railroads to a large extent for the transportation of oil. If the rail lines serving these people are going to be wrapped up, then should they develop trucking systems or a gathering system through the use of pipe lines? These are matters which will have to be planned for by the oil companies.
Another major problem concerns the municipalities themselves who might be affected by rail line abandonment. They have a co-operative or reciprocal agreement with their provincial government to develop transportation facilities, and this planning has been in force for a matter of ten years or more. If rail lines are to be abandoned and roads provided as an alternative to enable farmers to be able to market their grain, it will take several years of budgeting at large expense to the taxpayers in order to provide these facilities so that these people will not be too adversely affected by sudden change. These are some of the problems arising in connection with the procrastination and apparent indifference of the present government in dealing with this matter.
I do not want to labour this point, but I should like to say that No. 31 on the list of public bills is a bill standing in my name, Bill No. C-57, dealing with another aspect of rail line abandonment. I would urge the minister to bring in legislation to solve this problem and to give very serious consideration to the principles outlined in my proposed Bill No. C-57. I think that here is a concept or a principle which, if it is incorporated into government legislation, will help ease the blow when rail line abandonment becomes effective. I would ask the minister and his department to give special attention to this matter. I refer to my bill tonight because I do not think I will have the opportunity to do so later, due to the fact that my bill is so far down the list. Therefore, I again urge the government to take immediate, effective and active steps to develop this legislation. As I pointed out earlier in my remarks, the groundwork has been developed. The government do not have to do a lot of missionary work which the former government had to do. It is only a question of taking the bill which the former government prepared and perhaps with a few adjustments or amendments bring it before the house and pass it through. When this is done this heavy cloud of apprehension which is hanging over the people in western Canada will disperse.

Mr. Chairman, since we are dealing with the estimates of the Department of Agriculture, I feel duty bound to express my views on this subject which concerns the

greater part of the people of the riding of Lotbiniere. It is a fact that my constituency is essentially agricultural and does constitute one of the most typical of rural regions, where it is of the utmost importance to apply a well-defined agricultural policy.
Mr. Chairman, I have hardly been here a year, but I have found to my great disappointment that, when our Conservative friends criticize the agricultural policy of the present government-
You have none.

-the automatic reply from the lips of government members is this one: What prevented you from doing that during the five years you were in office?
Mr. Chairman, this is becoming childish and we sometimes hear people belonging to new parties say: We are under the impression that Conservatives and Liberals are anything but different. That is exactly the impression we should avoid.
As for farm policy, drastic reforms are imperative. Of course, a great deal of improvement has been made and I will have the opportunity, later on, to refute the authenticity of the figures quoted by the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Vincent) when he criticized the policy recently announced by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays).
Mr. Chairman, I feel that a drastic reform of agriculture is imperative and more particularly as far as eastern agriculture is concerned.

PROPOSED DIVERSION FROM HUDSON BAY INTO GREAT LAKES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Wednesday, May 6, I asked the right hon. Prime Minister if he had received from the Ontario chamber of commerce a resolution recommending to study the possibility of diverting the James bay waters into the great lakes, through the Harricanaw river, and if he intended to recommend that study. I

know that several other Canadian organizations are also interested in this matter. I want to ask him, tonight, and in his absence, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing), if, in the light of new developments and techniques, and especially in view of the need that is getting more pressing for soft water supply for the use of residents living near the great lakes, and in order, also, to correct several navigation problems on the St. Lawrence river and the Ottawa river, in the light of these facts, I would like to know whether the government expects to have technical and economic surveys made in that connection and whether it considers consulting the governments concerned, especially those of Quebec and Ontario, as well as the government of the United States, and of six or seven American states, concerning the project known as Grand Canal.
It is reported that the water level in the great lakes is going down continually; this is causing problems and the prospects are quite alarming. Besides, navigation on the St. Lawrence is seriously hindered, and this takes a heavy toll on the Canadian economy. This spring the press reported that the first ocean liner to leave the Montreal harbour had to reduce considerably its cargo before leaving port, because the water level was too low.
In the same line of thought, we are told that the reason why the water level is so dangerously low is the dry weather of last fall and the low precipitation during the winter. It still remains that last summer the water level in the harbour of Montreal and in the great lakes was lower than normal before the dry season.
Mr. Speaker, the government is certainly aware of the fact that an engineer from Sudbury, Ontario, has been making extended studies for several years to find an acceptable solution. He suggests the diversion of the Har-ricanaw river which has its source in lakes Senneville, Montigny, Malartic and Lamothe, in Abitibi, and flows into James bay after passing through Amos in my riding.
According to his project those waters would be forced back and diverted into lake Timis-kaming through a series of canals, dams and pumps. From there, the dredging of a canal cutting the line of watershed at North Bay would allow for the diversion of those waters into lake Nipissing, and from there into Georgian bay and the great lakes.
Mr. Speaker, you will understand that I am interested in that project since it directly affects my riding, and if it were carried out, it would be a significant improvement for the economy of that area which has been too much neglected by the authorities in the past.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: PROPOSED DIVERSION FROM HUDSON BAY INTO GREAT LAKES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. gentleman for his inquiry and to tell him this is a matter that is being taken exceedingly seriously by the government at the present time.
The more obvious losses on the great lakes to those who are operating resorts or carrying out shipping on them, are known to most of the people of Canada, but probably the most serious losses of all are not known to the people of Canada. We are reliably informed that the additional amount of coal which Ontario hydro had to buy last year because of the low levels in the lakes, and hence a reduction in power from hydro, was not less than $12 million. This was coal brought in to burn in thermal plants as a result of the low levels on the lakes. In addition to that, one of the most serious damages occurred not on the water but on the land in southern Ontario, and a reliable estimate states that last year over $75 million was lost in canning crops alone, as a result of the drought.
It is the contention of our branch and our water department that the principal reason for this is that we are in a very dry spell. There is a cycle of drought in the area of Ontario that normally feeds the lakes. In
1962	the rainfall was two inches less than it had been in the previous year, and that was almost two inches less than the average. In
1963	it was another three inches less, so that in two years there were five inches less rainfall in the area that feeds the lakes than there had been two years previously.
In addition to that we have had some very high temperatures during the last two years. The loss of water comes from two sources, namely lack of rainfall, and evaporation from the water that does fall, and for the past two years evaporation has been exceedingly high.
We are fully aware of the situation and have made a study. We are fully aware of the proposal in respect to the grand canal which envisions the use of power on the Nottaway river lying in the province of Quebec, which can produce a great deal of power, probably 900,000 kilowatts or 1 million kilowatts, to lifting water into the Har-ricanaw river behind dams, and changing the direction of the Harricanaw from flowing north and having it flow south.

subsubtopic: CHARGES BECAUSE OP LOW WATER LEVELS
speechtext:
My question hinges upon something the minister of northern affairs has already touched upon, although it has an entirely different twang to it; it has a western flavour. I have raised this question because nobody heretofore has raised the question that, with the water levels low, it has affected the western economy.
My point of contention is that because of the low levels of the great lakes boats coming in for loading have had to fill to less than 100 per cent capacity. They have had to take on partial loads. This, in effect, has had the result that more boats have had to come in, and as a result of more boats having to come in this means that we, as western producers- and I speak as a western producer, a western farmer, myself-will have to pay the cost of more boats coming in. I think whether the government realizes this or not the western farmer is conscious of what is happening in central Canada. Whether central Canada is interested in western Canada or not, western Canada is interested in the economy of the central part of that area which is supposed to be immune to all our suggestions and so on.
What I am suggesting at the moment is that neither the minister nor the government has taken into consideration the problem that we have, namely that we are being charged for delivery of grain to foreign countries. It seems that we have a very good product, one that is saleable, and I am sure the Minister of Trade and Commerce who is presently out of the country is interested in selling our product. But he has not taken cognizance of the problem that we have in Canada. We have tried to promote sales abroad, yet we do not do anything about our problem right here in Canada.
How do we keep the cost of selling our product at such a level as to be competitive? By keeping our product competitive, I mean can we sell it to another country by utilizing the maximum of our shipping capacity? These are ways that will prove to the western producers that the government is interested in their welfare; these are ways that will prove to all, not necessarily to the western producer but to all Canadians, that the government is interested in doing something to re-
[Mr. Laing.l

move the balance of trade problem which has faced not only this government but the previous government; and I think this government should take a close look at the problem.
We are very much concerned over the fact that the port of Churchill, for example, has not been utilized to its maximum and I notice that out of 67 days, when we had a shipping season, 15 days were not used. It seems to me that this is the root of the problem. Are we making maximum use of efficiency? Are we placing our product on the world market in such a way that it is competitive? If we had used up the days at Churchill we could have saved 12 cents a bushel on every bushel that was exported out of Canada by using the maximum facilities we had. Even out of the terminals at the great lakes, we should have saved. But what do we do? We bring in two boats instead of one-intead of bringing in one boat and filling it to capacity. It is very easy: You bring in a boat, load it to half capacity. Oh, temporarily you give somebody work for the time being, but what do you do in the meantime? Do you protect the saleability of the product? Not only is wheat in question; the point is that every product we have in Canada is affected. Perhaps I could read this quotation from the Sun-Times of April 6:
Captain Bert Bazeley, fleet manager for Upper Lakes Shipping Ltd., Toronto, says each of the company's ten large carriers is shipping 1,000 tons light every trip.
That is because they have trouble getting into ports. It seems to me this is not only a question of shipping grain out of lake Superior or any of our other ports, but this problem applies to every product that we manufacture or produce. I think the question I have raised is important enough to be given serious consideration when we are trying to get into the world market. If we have a product to sell-and we have a great many good products to sell-I think the government should recognize the fact that they are not doing anything to promote the sale of these products or enable those who produce the products to sell them, because of the situation that exists.
I think the government should recognize this problem and do something to solve it, whether dredging is needed or whatever it is. I certainly do not agree with the theory that we should pray for rain, and I think now is the time for the government to come up with some sort of policy.
